members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:
Where the open indicator sits, or whether there is one.

`auto` resolves to `end`, which is where a reader scanning a list of
summaries expects it: the label starts at the same x on every row, and the
indicator is found once at the edge rather than shifting with the text.
`start` is for a tree-like reading, where the indicator leads the label.
`none` is for a row that carries its own affordance and would otherwise
have two.

members.name: renderChevron
members.description: The chevron, or nothing when suppressed.

members.name: accordion
members.description:
The nearest accordion above this item, if there is one.

Resolved on demand rather than held, so an item moved between accordions
coordinates with the one it is in now. `closest` crosses no shadow
boundary, which is correct: an item inside another item's content is in
that item's light DOM and finds the same accordion, so the check below is
what keeps it independent.

members.name: peers
members.description:
The items this one coordinates with: its own siblings, and only those.

Direct children only. An accordion nested inside an item's content is a
separate set, and opening a section in it must not close anything outside.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Opens or closes this item, and enforces the accordion's mode.

The item that was clicked is the coordinator. It refuses first, then
announces, then applies, then closes its peers, in that order: closing a
peer before knowing whether this change was even allowed would leave the
set collapsed after a listener refused it.

members.name: focusTrigger
members.description:
Moves focus to this item's trigger.

The parent accordion drives arrow-key navigation and cannot reach the
trigger itself, because it is inside this item's shadow root. Exposing the
intent as a method keeps the parent out of the child's internals.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: separation
members.description:
How the stack separates itself from the page.

Two of the axis's four values, which is what this surface has meaning for:
a stack of items is already told apart by its seams, so a lift would be a
third statement and a fill a second.

- `plain` is the default and is what an application usually wants: the
  seams between items already say the items are one set, so a frame is a
  second statement of the same thing. Inside a card, a panel, a dialog or a
  sidebar, it is a line and no meaning.
- `outlined` frames the stack, for an accordion sitting directly on the
  page where nothing else says where it starts and stops. A marketing
  page's FAQ is the case it is for.

Both are writable, so a generated page can say which it means rather than
relying on the absence of an attribute.

members.name: mode
members.description:
How many sections may be open at once.

Absent is `multiple`, so nothing closes unexpectedly and the default costs
no attribute on the host. `single` keeps exactly one open and refuses to
close the last; `single-collapsible` keeps at most one and lets it close.

A union rather than a mode plus a `collapsible` boolean, which would make
`collapsible` alongside `multiple` expressible and meaningless.

members.name: tone
members.description:
Which color the band wears.

**This was `severity` and it was claiming more than it did.** Severity is a
judgement about the message, and elsewhere in this library it carries one:
`Callout` reads `TONE_MARKS` for an icon and a label, so `tone="danger"`
puts a mark beside the text and names it to a screen reader. Here it did
none of that. It set a color, the live region stayed polite either way, and
nothing about the announcement's semantics moved. A property that only
changes the paint should say so.

`tone` is the word this library already uses for exactly that, and `Tag`
made the identical rename for the identical reason: the word it left was a
treatment, `tone` is semantic color. The set matches `Tag`'s so the two
agree, with `neutral` as the resting value and `primary` for a band that is
about the product rather than about a state.

`neutral` is what an unset announcement already looked like, said out loud
so a consumer can put a band back to it from markup, and `surface` is the
one value that is not a color: it lifts the band onto the surface step
instead of the sunken one, for a strip carrying something that is not a
state at all.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the `actions` region whether anything is in it.

An empty region is not free: it is still a flex item, so it still takes the
container's gap. There is no selector that can ask, `slot:empty` being
about a slot's fallback rather than its assigned nodes, so the component
asks and says so, on the region inside this shadow root rather than on the
host: an attribute written onto the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration and does not patch up.

members.name: renderDismissIcon
members.description:
The cross inside the dismiss button, behind a seam.

Slot fallback, so a consumer replaces it by slotting; and a method, so the
tier above replaces it by overriding. Those answer different people: the
slot is for the page and the method is for whoever is building the styled
layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

**Named for what it draws, which it was not.** It was `renderIcon`, with a
description of "the mark for the announcement's tone", and it draws the `x`
glyph inside the dismiss button and has never drawn a tone. The name is
`renderIcon` on `Toast` and `Callout` too, and on both of those it takes a
severity and draws exactly the tone mark this claimed to: the prose came
from a sibling that meant it. An announcement has no tone mark at all.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the banner is made of, which is how much of what is behind it shows
through.

One axis, three points, and absent is opaque, per the rule that a reflected
property takes no default.

- Absent is opaque. The page stops at the bar, which is what an application
  wants: the bar is chrome and chrome does not need to be interesting.
- `glass` is translucent and blurred, so content passing underneath stays
  visible and goes soft. The page reads as one surface with a bar floating
  over it.
- `transparent` has no fill at all until something has scrolled under it,
  and then it takes the glass. For a banner over a hero, where the art
  should reach the top of the window and the bar should only become a
  surface once it has to be legible over moving content.

**This was `appearance`, and it was filed under the wrong axis from the
start.** The library's test is the one `Card` states: `separation` is where
a surface ends, `tone` is what it means, `material` is what it is made of,
and a property belongs to `material` when it can be true at the same time
as the other two. Every value here varies exactly one quantity, and that
quantity is translucency. The proof is inside the component rather than in
the argument: scrolled, `transparent` emits the same two declarations

members.name: sticky
members.description:

than about the bar, and because a reflected `true` writes an attribute the
server's markup does not have. Every default here is the absent attribute.

top of the page, so `glass` and `transparent` have nothing to be
translucent against and `data-scrolled` never lands.

members.name: contentAlign
members.description:
Where the middle region sits in the bar.

Centered by default, which reads as the site's spine when the navigation is
the primary thing in the header rather than an afterthought beside a logo.
Centered against the banner rather than against whatever space the brand
left over, so the middle of the nav is the middle of the window whatever
the wordmark and the actions happen to measure.

`start` is the opt-out, for a header whose middle region trails the brand.

**Named for the region and not for what is usually in it.** It was
`nav-align`, which reads as a property about `Navigation` and is not: the
middle slot takes whatever a consumer puts there, a search field or a
breadcrumb trail as readily as a nav, and a header that centred its search
box would have been setting `nav-align` to do it. The part is called
`content`, so the property is too.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
A band rather than a line, so the fill cannot flicker at the boundary.

**`scrollY > 0` is a threshold with no width, and a threshold with no width
is a switch sitting exactly where scroll positions cluster.** Zero is not a
quiet place: rubber-banding overshoots past it and comes back, scroll
anchoring nudges by a pixel when an image or a font lands, and a
`scroll-behavior: smooth` jump settles by oscillating around its target.

blur are both transitioned, so each toggle started a fresh animation in the
opposite direction. What a reader sees is a bar that shimmers, and text
legible through it for as long as the fill is part way in.

Eight pixels to take the fill, two to give it back. Asymmetric on purpose:
the bar should look attached to the top of the page for as long as it
honestly is, so leaving is nearly the whole way back, and arriving needs
enough travel to mean the reader moved rather than the layout did.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

The same app header on the headless tier, with every rule written by hand.
Blurred over what scrolls beneath it.

Over a dark hero, taking its own colour mode.

declarations.name: exitOf

parameters.name: tilt
parameters.description: The angle handed to the shader, in degrees.

parameters.name: aspect
parameters.description: The box's width over its height.

declarations.description:
Where the shader's axis crosses the top edge, as a fraction of the width.

Follows `main()` in `aura-shader.ts`:

1. `p.x *= aspect` stretches the frame before anything rotates, so the tilt
   the rotation takes is a slope in the stretched frame rather than on
   screen.
2. `float a = atan(sin(want), cos(want) * aspect)` is the angle it actually
   turns by, which is the asked-for screen angle converted into that frame.
3. `mat2 turn = mat2(cos(a), sin(a), -sin(a), cos(a))` rotates, and the axis
   is the line the rotated x is zero on: `cos(a) * x - sin(a) * y = 0`.

At the top edge `y` is 1, so the crossing is at `x = tan(a)` in the stretched
frame, and dividing the stretch back out puts it on screen. The aspect is
therefore paid twice, once going into the rotation and once coming out, which
is why it appears squared when the three steps are collapsed.

declarations.name: tiltFor

parameters.name: terminus
parameters.description: The crossing wanted, as a fraction of the width.

parameters.name: aspect
parameters.description: The box's width over its height.

declarations.description:
The tilt, in degrees, whose axis crosses the top edge at `terminus`.

The inverse of `exitOf`, solved rather than fitted: collapsing its three
steps gives `terminus = 0.5 + tan(tilt) / (2 * aspect^2)`, and rearranging
for the tilt gives what is below.

This is the contract `terminus` has always claimed and twice failed to keep:
`0` is the left edge, `0.5` the middle and `1` the right edge, in every box.

One fragment shader over a full-screen triangle, with the palette read from
the tokens rather than given as colors. That is the whole reason this belongs
in a design system instead of in a page: a background written with hex values
is an asset that has to be re-cut when the brand moves, and one written
against `--helix-color-primary` is a consequence of it.

**Every shape ramps through four token stops**, and the token layer inverts
each of them: the page's own background, `primary-subtle`, `primary`, and
then a peak. The peak is the foreground on a dark page and `primary-active`
on a light one, because mixing a saturated hue toward near-black takes the
chroma out of exactly the pixels carrying the most of it. Which way the page
runs is not asked of the mode, which is a private token: it is read off the
ground's own luminance, which the shader already has.

**No dependency, and no scene graph.** The geometry is three vertices derived
from `gl_VertexID`, so there is no attribute, no buffer and no upload. The
common implementations of this reach for a 3D library to draw one quad, which
is a camera and a material system for four vertices that never move.

**It stops when nobody is looking**, off screen and in a background tab, and
`prefers-reduced-motion` gets one still frame rather than an empty box: the
composition is the point and the drift is a garnish.

**A layer over an interactive aura has to let the pointer through.** The
element is hit-testable only when `interactive` is set, because a background
that swallows clicks is worse than one that does nothing, but a scrim or an
overlay a consumer paints on top will absorb the move before it arrives. Any
decorative layer above this wants `pointer-events: none`. It has already
caught this repository's own bench once.

**The fallback needs no detection.** Where WebGL is refused the canvas never
paints and is transparent, and the host carries a gradient of the same tokens
underneath. Nothing has to ask whether it worked.

Presentation only, so there is no headless tier: the split exists to keep
behavior separate from styling, and there is no structure or semantics here
to separate. Decorative, so the host is hidden from assistive technology and
takes no pointer events.
declarations.name: HelixAura

cssParts.description: The surface the shader draws into.
cssParts.name: canvas

members.name: shape
members.description:
Which form the light takes. Absent is `braid`.

Reflected because the fallback gradient selects on it, and given no default
for the same reason every axis here has none: a default on a reflected
property writes the attribute onto every host anybody renders.

members.name: drift
members.description:
How far the settings wander on their own, `0` still and `1` restless.

**One property rather than a range on each of the five.** A range per axis
is five more things to author and four more chances to write a pair that
fights another; the reason to want any of it is the same reason in every
case, which is that a fixed field is legibly a loop. So this is an amount,
and each axis is given its own span and its own period.

The periods are irrational multiples of each other, so no two axes come
back into phase and the field has no cycle a reader can count. That is the
difference between a background that breathes and one that is obviously on
a timer.

members.name: interaction
members.description:
What the pointer does, where the shape's own answer is not wanted.

Absent is `native`, which is each shape answering in the terms it is made
of: braid leans, rays are occluded, threads pinch, particles scatter. The
named options are generic, and are a deliberate step down in meaning. A
response made of the same material as the shape says something about that
shape; a lamp following the cursor says the same nothing on all nine.

They exist because a consumer may want the quieter, more conventional
answer, and because `none` is a real requirement. Not because any of them
is the better default.

members.name: reach
members.description:
How far the pointer reaches into the field, `0` upward.

Multiplied into the presence the pointer already fades in and out with, so
it scales the whole response rather than any one part of it, whichever
interaction is in play.

members.name: interactive
members.description:
Whether the pointer shifts and lifts the field.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it: a background is not
hit-testable at rest, or it would swallow clicks meant for what is over it,
and an element that is not hit-testable never receives the `pointermove`
this listens for. Asking for the pointer is asking for the hit test.

members.name: bloom
members.description: How soft the falloff is, `0` tight and `1` diffuse.

members.name: gain
members.description: Overall brightness, as a multiplier on the field.

members.name: scale
members.description: Feature size, as a multiplier on the sampled coordinates.

members.name: speed
members.description: How fast it drifts, as a multiplier on time.

members.name: tilt
members.description: The field's rotation, in degrees.

members.name: terminus
members.description:
Where the axis crosses the top edge, as a fraction of the width.

**An angle does not say what a consumer means, and this does.** The axis
runs `x = y * tan(tilt)`, so the same `tilt` puts the exit somewhere else
the moment the box changes shape. Measured on the landing page hero, which
was tuned to 23 degrees against a box two screens tall: at a 1152 pixel
window that lands the exit at 979, between the navigation and the actions,
and at a 720 pixel window it lands at 611, a third of the way further left.
Nothing is wrong with either number and neither is what anybody asked for.

Given as a fraction rather than a length so it survives the same change:
`0` is the left edge, `0.5` the middle and `1` the right edge, at every
size. Absent leaves `tilt` in charge, so an angle is still sayable where
the angle really is the point, which is what an aura in a square tile
wants.

**The fraction is measured across the whole width, and for a while it was
not.** The first expression corrected for the aspect once in the wrong
direction and never subtracted the centre, so the value read as an offset
from the middle that also moved with the box: on a 1440 by 1800 hero `0.5`
put the axis at 81.3% of the width and `0` was the only value that reached
the middle. The contract above is now solved against what the shader draws
rather than asserted beside it.

Derived from the box the resize observer already keeps, so it costs no
layout read per frame, and the drift is applied to the result rather than
to the angle behind it: the field still wanders, around a bearing that
holds the exit where it was put.

members.name: variance
members.description:
How much the members of a population differ from one another, `0` a set
that is uniform and `1` the resting amount. Clamped to that range: these
are interpolations, so a larger number extrapolates rather than
exaggerating, and a streak whose length has passed through zero is drawn
as a bar across the whole frame.

Read by the shapes made of many similar things, whether those are counted
or continuous: `streaks`, whose lanes draw a speed, a length, a width, a
spacing and a weight apiece; `particles`, whose motes draw a size, a
brightness and a wander; and `rays` and `aurora`, whose fan, bundles and
folds widen or even out. `braid`, `waves` and `flow` have a
single subject and nothing to vary, and `threads` is even on purpose, so on
those four this is inert.

members.name: tokens
members.description: Repaints when the palette moves, which no re-render would do on its own.

members.name: palette

type.text: { glow: TokenColor; ground: TokenColor; haze: TokenColor; peak: TokenColor }

members.description:
The four ramp stops, resolved.

**Cached, because reading them is not free and they do not move.** Each
read sets a style, calls `getComputedStyle`, fills a pixel and reads it
back: a style recalc and a canvas readback apiece. Doing that inside
`paint` meant four of each on every frame, forever, to fetch values that
change only when the color mode does. The controller already says when
that happens, so this is filled from there and from the first paint.

members.name: trail
members.description:
Where the pointer has been, as flat triples of x, y and age.

A ring rather than a queue: the oldest slot is overwritten, so nothing is
allocated and the cost is the same on the first second and the thousandth.

members.name: ordered
members.description:
The same marks, oldest first, which is what the shader is given.

The ring's own order is not time order, and the wake is drawn as a polyline
through consecutive entries: a segment across the wrap joined the newest
mark to the oldest and drew a bright bar clean through the middle of the
field. Unrolled once per frame, which is eight copies.

members.name: head
members.description:
The live end of the stroke, outside the ring.

**In the ring it destroyed a mark every time it committed.** The head was
the slot at `trailNext`, so advancing wrote over whatever was oldest, and
the tail of the stroke lost a point instantly rather than fading. Held
apart, committing appends where the head already is: the polyline goes from
ending at P to ending at P, P, which is the same shape, and nothing jumps.

members.name: target
members.description: Where the pointer is, and where the field has got to. The gap is weight.

members.name: box
members.description:
The element's box, cached.

**Read per event, this was the ragged half.** `getBoundingClientRect` forces
a synchronous layout, and a pointer emits events far faster than the
display refreshes: a 1000Hz mouse flushed layout a thousand times a second
to compute a number that only changes when the page reflows. Refreshed from
the resize observer and from scroll, both of which are exactly when it can
go stale, and never from the handler that reads it.

members.name: sized
members.description: Watches the element's own size, so no frame has to ask for it.

members.name: readPalette
members.description:
Resolves the ramp. Called when the palette moves, not when a frame draws.

Light pages peak on a deep brand blue and dark ones on the foreground, and
the ground is what says which: mixing a saturated hue toward near-black
takes the chroma out of exactly the pixels carrying the most of it. Read
from the ground's own luminance rather than asked of the color mode, which
is a private token this tier may not reach for.

members.name: measure
members.description:
Re-reads the box and resizes the drawing buffer to match.

**Called from the observer, never from the frame.** `clientWidth` is a
layout read, and doing it in `tick` meant a forced synchronous layout on
every single frame to learn a number that changes when the box changes and
at no other time. A `ResizeObserver` is told when that is.

members.name: paintOnce
members.description: One frame, now, for a change that has to show while the loop is stopped.

members.name: bearing
members.description:
The angle actually drawn, which is `terminus` resolved against the box.

A getter rather than a stored value because the box changes and this has no
business knowing when: it is read once per frame from numbers already
there.

The solve is `tiltFor` in `aura-axis.ts` rather than an expression here,
and that is the fix for how this went wrong twice. Both times the
arithmetic sat inside this getter next to a sentence describing different
arithmetic, and nothing in the repository could tell they disagreed. It is
callable now, and `aura-root.dom.spec.ts` runs it against a model of the
shader in both directions. See 155.

members.name: age
members.description: Ages the wake, and drops a fresh mark where the pointer has moved far.

members.name: advanceWake
members.description:
Keeps the head of the wake on the cursor, and commits it as it travels.

**The head used to be a committed mark, and that was both faults at once.**
Marks are spaced by distance so eight slots cover a gesture rather than the
last few milliseconds of one, but committing was also the only time the
stroke grew: its leading end therefore sat up to a full gate behind the
pointer, and caught up in jumps of exactly that size. Latent, and jagged,
for one reason.

So the slot at `trailNext` is provisional. It is rewritten every frame to
wherever the field has actually eased to, which is where the cursor looks
like it is, so the stroke always reaches the pointer. Crossing the gate does
not move the head, it just stops the previous position from being
overwritten, and a new provisional head starts from there. The wake grows
continuously and is still only ever eight points.

Measured against `eased` rather than `target`, or the stroke would reach a
place the field has not arrived at yet and lead its own parallax.

Multiplied into the presence the pointer already fades in and out with, so
it scales the whole response rather than any one part of it, whichever
interaction is in play.

attributes.name: interactive
attributes.description:
Whether the pointer shifts and lifts the field.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it: a background is not
hit-testable at rest, or it would swallow clicks meant for what is over it,
and an element that is not hit-testable never receives the `pointermove`
this listens for. Asking for the pointer is asking for the hit test.

attributes.name: bloom
attributes.description: How soft the falloff is, `0` tight and `1` diffuse.

attributes.name: gain
attributes.description: Overall brightness, as a multiplier on the field.

attributes.name: scale
attributes.description: Feature size, as a multiplier on the sampled coordinates.

attributes.name: speed
attributes.description: How fast it drifts, as a multiplier on time.

attributes.name: tilt
attributes.description: The field's rotation, in degrees.

attributes.name: terminus
attributes.description:
Where the axis crosses the top edge, as a fraction of the width.

**An angle does not say what a consumer means, and this does.** The axis
runs `x = y * tan(tilt)`, so the same `tilt` puts the exit somewhere else
the moment the box changes shape. Measured on the landing page hero, which
was tuned to 23 degrees against a box two screens tall: at a 1152 pixel
window that lands the exit at 979, between the navigation and the actions,
and at a 720 pixel window it lands at 611, a third of the way further left.
Nothing is wrong with either number and neither is what anybody asked for.

Given as a fraction rather than a length so it survives the same change:
`0` is the left edge, `0.5` the middle and `1` the right edge, at every
size. Absent leaves `tilt` in charge, so an angle is still sayable where
the angle really is the point, which is what an aura in a square tile
wants.

**The fraction is measured across the whole width, and for a while it was
not.** The first expression corrected for the aspect once in the wrong
direction and never subtracted the centre, so the value read as an offset
from the middle that also moved with the box: on a 1440 by 1800 hero `0.5`
put the axis at 81.3% of the width and `0` was the only value that reached
the middle. The contract above is now solved against what the shader draws
rather than asserted beside it.

Derived from the box the resize observer already keeps, so it costs no
layout read per frame, and the drift is applied to the result rather than
to the angle behind it: the field still wanders, around a bearing that
holds the exit where it was put.

attributes.name: variance
attributes.description:
How much the members of a population differ from one another, `0` a set
that is uniform and `1` the resting amount. Clamped to that range: these
are interpolations, so a larger number extrapolates rather than
exaggerating, and a streak whose length has passed through zero is drawn
as a bar across the whole frame.

Read by the shapes made of many similar things, whether those are counted
or continuous: `streaks`, whose lanes draw a speed, a length, a width, a
spacing and a weight apiece; `particles`, whose motes draw a size, a
brightness and a wander; and `rays` and `aurora`, whose fan, bundles and
folds widen or even out. `braid`, `waves` and `flow` have a
single subject and nothing to vary, and `threads` is even on purpose, so on
those four this is inert.

declarations.summary: A lit, drifting background, drawn from the token layer.

examples.description: A braided shaft of light, sized by the box it is put in.
Curtains on a drifting horizon, the one shape that is a landscape.
Light through moving water. The pointer is a stone dropped in it.
Every setting wandering on its own period, so the field has no countable cycle.
Ink in a viscous medium. Move the pointer and the wake outlives it.
Territories, lit only along the seams where two of them meet.
A structure in perspective, lit at its joints.
Points adrift on their own orbits, pushed aside by the pointer.
The field answering a pointer, and how far its reach carries.
Rays from a source above the frame, following the pointer.
Light travelling in lanes. The pointer is an obstacle the trails bow around.
Where the light leaves the top edge, held there whatever the box does.
Five curves woven to a pinch, and the pointer carries the pinch.
The same braid, wound tighter and lit harder.
Broad bands rolling under a warp, with the crests dragged by the pointer.

declarations.name: SHAPES
declarations.description:
The shapes, in the order the shader branches on them.

Exported so the component can turn a property into the integer the uniform
takes without a second list to keep in step.

declarations.name: INTERACTIONS
declarations.description:
What the pointer does, in the order the shader branches on them.

`native` is the shape's own, and is what absence means: braid leans, rays are
occluded, threads pinch. The rest are generic, and deliberately few.

**The generics are the thing this component spent a day removing**, so they
are opt-in and never a default. A response made of the same material as the
shape says something about that shape; a lamp that follows the cursor says
the same nothing on all nine. They are here because a consumer may want the
quieter, more conventional answer, not because it is the better one.

declarations.name: VERTEX
declarations.default: `#version 300 es out vec2 uv; void main() { vec2 p = vec2((gl_VertexID << 1) & 2, gl_VertexID & 2); uv = p; gl_Position = vec4(p * 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0); } `
declarations.description:
Three vertices from `gl_VertexID`, covering the screen with one triangle.

No attribute, no buffer and no upload, and one triangle rather than two, so
there is no seam down the diagonal where a quad's halves meet.

declarations.name: FRAGMENT
declarations.default: `#version 300 es precision highp float; in vec2 uv; out vec4 color; uniform vec2 uResolution; uniform float uTime; uniform int uShape; uniform vec2 uPointer; uniform float uReach; uniform int uInteraction; uniform float uTilt; uniform float uScale; uniform float uBloom; uniform float uGain; /* How much the members of a population differ from one another, 1 being the resting amount and 0 a set that is uniform. Read by the shapes made of many similar things, whether those are counted or continuous: streaks has lanes, particles has motes, rays has a fan, and aurora has bundles and folds. Braid, waves and flow have a single subject and nothing to vary. Threads is the deliberate exception, being even on purpose: a pass had already given its strands their own hashes and produced a scatter rather than a set. */ uniform float uVariance; /* Where the pointer has been, as x, y and age. Age runs 0 at the moment it was left to 1 when it has faded, so a spent slot costs a compare. **This is what a fluid gets from a framebuffer, bought for eight vec3s.** A real solver advects a dye texture and reads it back the next frame, which needs render targets, a ping-pong pair and about six passes. What a reader actually perceives from that is one thing: the cursor leaves a wake that outlives it. A short history of where it went reproduces that in the single pass this component already makes, at a fixed cost that does not grow with how long the page has been open. What it cannot do is conserve anything, so there is no diffusion and no pressure: the wake decays rather than spreading. Worth knowing before this is asked to be a simulation. */ uniform vec3 uTrail[9]; uniform vec3 uGround; uniform vec3 uHaze; uniform vec3 uGlow; uniform vec3 uPeak; float hash(vec2 p) { return fract(sin(dot(p, vec2(127.1, 311.7))) * 43758.5453123); } float noise(vec2 p) { vec2 i = floor(p); vec2 f = fract(p); /* Quintic rather than cubic. Cubic smoothstep leaves a second derivative discontinuity at every cell edge, which four octaves of lighting turn into a faint square lattice: visible on a large soft field and exactly the artifact that reads as cheap. */ vec2 u = f * f * f * (f * (f * 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0); return mix( mix(hash(i), hash(i + vec2(1.0, 0.0)), u.x), mix(hash(i + vec2(0.0, 1.0)), hash(i + vec2(1.0, 1.0)), u.x), u.y ); } /* Each octave is rotated as well as scaled. Doubling alone stacks every octave on the same axes, so value noise keeps its grid however many are summed. An irrational angle means no two octaves ever line up again. */ const mat2 TURN = mat2(0.8, 0.6, -0.6, 0.8); float fbm(vec2 p) { float sum = 0.0; float amp = 0.5; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { sum += amp * noise(p); p = TURN * p * 2.03; amp *= 0.5; } return sum; } /* Domain warping: the field is sampled at coordinates another field bends. This is the single largest difference between noise that reads as organic and noise that reads as television static, and it costs two more fbm calls rather than a different algorithm. */ float warped(vec2 p, float t) { vec2 q = vec2(fbm(p + vec2(0.0, t)), fbm(p + vec2(5.2, 1.3 - t))); vec2 r = vec2(fbm(p + 4.0 * q + vec2(1.7, 9.2)), fbm(p + 4.0 * q + vec2(8.3, 2.8))); return fbm(p + 4.0 * r); } /* An exponential falloff without the corner. * * Both abs and length have a vertex at zero and their derivative jumps * across it, so a falloff built on either acquires a hard line exactly along * the axis it is brightest on. That is a crease in something meant to be * light, and it is what put a chevron through the braid wherever the * pointer's height crossed a strand. * * Softening the distance rather than the exponent keeps the tails identical * and rounds only the point. The softening scales with the rate, so a tight * falloff is rounded tightly and a broad one broadly: at zero the result is * exp(-0.06) whatever the rate is, six per cent off the peak, which is not * visible as flattening. * * Takes the squared distance, because every caller already has one and a * square root taken here is the one that would have reintroduced the vertex. */ float falloff(float d2, float k) { float soft = 0.06 / k; return exp(-sqrt(d2 + soft * soft) * k); } /* Two strands half a turn apart, inside a wider volume. */ float braid(vec2 q, float t, vec2 qp, float reach) { /* The strands lean toward the pointer where it is alongside them, and are unmoved where it is not. A braid is a thing with a length, so what it can answer with is a bend at a height, not a bulge at a point. */ float alongside = falloff((q.y - qp.y) * (q.y - qp.y), 1.1) * reach; float lean = qp.x * alongside * 0.45; float lit = 0.0; for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { float phase = float(i) * 3.14159265; float x = q.x - lean - 0.34 * sin(q.y * 1.6 + t * 1.4 + phase); lit += 0.8 * falloff(x * x, 13.0); } float volume = falloff(q.x * q.x, 2.6); /* Compressed hard across the shaft and stretched along it. The same octaves sampled square read as haze; this way they read as filaments. */ float streak = fbm(vec2(q.x * 9.0, q.y * 0.55 - t * 2.4)); float haze = warped(vec2(q.x * 0.8 + 4.0, q.y * 0.45), t * 0.5); return lit * mix(0.35, 1.65, streak) + volume * 0.3 * mix(0.35, 1.05, haze); } /* A fan from a source above the frame, cut into filaments by angle. */ float rays(vec2 q, float t, vec2 qp, float reach) { /* The pointer occludes, rather than the source moving. Swinging the source re-aimed the whole fan, which is a thing a light does and not a thing that happens when something passes in front of one. What a reader knows about rays is that an object crossing them takes a bite out of the light and drags a shadow behind itself, away from the source. So the source is fixed and the pointer is a blocker. The shadow is angular, not radial: it is the wedge of directions the object covers as seen from the source, and it only exists further along than the object is. A fragment nearer the source than the blocker is in front of it and stays lit, which is the whole difference between an occluder and a dark patch that follows the cursor. */ vec2 o = vec2(0.0, 1.45); vec2 v = q - o; float dist = length(v); float ang = atan(v.x, -v.y); vec2 vp = qp - o; float distToBlocker = length(vp); float angToBlocker = atan(vp.x, -vp.y); /* Widened with distance, so the object reads as a fixed size rather than as a wedge that grows the further out it is carried. */ float halfAngle = 0.055 / max(distToBlocker, 0.35); float across = (ang - angToBlocker) / halfAngle; /* Cast from the near edge of the object rather than from somewhere past it. Ramping in over a fifth of a unit started the shadow below the thing supposedly casting it, which reads as two objects. */ float behind = smoothstep(-0.03, 0.05, dist - distToBlocker); float shadow = exp(-across * across) * behind * reach; float fan = fbm(vec2(ang * 8.0, dist * 0.5 - t * 1.8)); float dust = warped(vec2(ang * 2.0, dist * 0.7), t * 0.4); float spread = smoothstep(0.85, 0.05, abs(ang)); /* The fan is a population too, even though it is continuous rather than counted: how far apart its light and dark run is how much one ray differs from the next. Both ends travel toward the midpoint, so a variance of 0 is an even wash and a variance of 1 is exactly the pair this always had. */ float rv = clamp(uVariance, 0.0, 1.0); float lit = spread * mix(mix(0.85, 0.2, rv), mix(0.85, 1.5, rv), fan) * mix(0.75, 1.15, dust) * falloff(dot(v, v), 0.8); return lit * (1.0 - shadow * 0.82); } /* Curtains on a drifting horizon. */ float aurora(vec2 q, float t, vec2 qp, float reach) { /* The curtain waves harder where the pointer is, rather than being lifted by it. An aurora is a sheet with an amplitude, and a swell only raised the whole thing locally, which is a bump in a line. Multiplying the amplitude bends it instead: the folds deepen and the ridge travels further, which is what an aurora does when it is disturbed. */ float agitate = falloff((q.x - qp.x) * (q.x - qp.x), 1.5) * reach; /* A curtain stands. It does not hang. This was a falloff symmetric about the ridge, which is a band with a wavy centre line, and a band with vertical noise on it is an equaliser. An aurora has a sharp lower border where the field lines reach their lowest, and light that thins upward from it, so the top and the bottom cannot be the same function. Cut hard below, drawn long above. Two of them, offset and at different depths, because a single sheet reads as a decal and what makes the real thing look like drapery is one curtain seen through another. */ float lit = 0.0; for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { float f = float(i); /* Two octaves, not a warp. A warp folds the domain back on itself and puts high frequencies in the ridge, and against a hard top edge every wiggle becomes a spike: the first pass came out a mountain range. What an aurora has is a long undulation with a few folds in it, which is what a low fundamental and one overtone give. */ float ridge = ((noise(vec2(q.x * (0.55 + f * 0.2) + f * 4.0, t * 0.3)) - 0.5) * 1.7 + (noise(vec2(q.x * (1.3 + f * 0.4) + f * 9.0, t * 0.45)) - 0.5) * 0.55) * (1.0 + agitate * 2.0) + f * 0.22; /* **The sheet stands on the ridge rather than hanging from it, and that inversion is the whole difference between an aurora and a landscape.** A hard edge with mass under it is a mountain silhouette, which is exactly what this drew: one unbroken ridge line across the frame with a striped solid below it. The real thing is the other way up. A curtain's lower border is its sharpest, brightest line, and what rises from it thins and breaks into rays. Nothing else here had to change. */ float depth = q.y - ridge; /* Sharp, but not a cliff: the edge is where the light stops, and a step narrower than a pixel is an aliased line rather than an edge. */ /* **The border's sharpness varies along it.** One constant made one continuously crisp line across the whole curtain, and a line of even weight reads as drawn rather than lit however it wanders. A real lower border is hard where the sheet faces us and diffuse where it turns away, so the crispness is drawn from the same slow noise the folds are. */ float crisp = mix(0.04, 0.3, noise(vec2(q.x * 0.8 + f * 5.0, t * 0.15))); float edge = smoothstep(-crisp, crisp * 0.5, depth); /* Steeper, so the curtain thins instead of filling everything above the border. At 1.5 it still stood at a fifth a whole unit up, which with the bundles over it painted a solid wall of stripes from the border to the top of the frame: the dark under a hard line then read as a hill and the light over it as rain. A curtain is mostly the bottom of a curtain. */ float rise = exp(-max(depth, 0.0) * (2.9 + f * 1.1)); /* Stretched hard along the fall, so the striations are the vertical rays a curtain is actually made of rather than texture on a stripe. */ /* 0.9 along the fall, not 0.35. Stretched that hard the rays held one value for their whole length, which is a picket fence however the bundles are shaped: what varies along a ray is the thing that makes it look like moving light rather than a printed stripe. */ float rays = fbm(vec2(q.x * (9.0 + f * 4.0), q.y * 0.9 - t * (2.2 + f))); /* A rim along the top edge. The brightest part of a curtain is the line where the field lines end, and without it the sheet fades in from nothing and reads as fog with stripes rather than as something with a boundary. Wide enough to see: at k = 26 this was two pixels and might as well not have been there. */ float rim = falloff(depth * depth, 7.0) * 0.45; /* **A curtain is not the width of the sky.** Running edge to edge is what made the ridge read as a horizon: a horizon is continuous and a curtain is not. Broken into lengths by a slow mask, with real gaps between them, it becomes some number of curtains rather than one long one. */ float lengths = smoothstep(0.2, 0.66, noise(vec2(q.x * 1.15 + f * 13.0, t * 0.12))); /* Rays clump. Straight fbm is evenly spaced striping, which is a picket fence whatever else is done to it, and the floor under it lit the sheet everywhere so the rays only ever read as texture on a solid band. Pushing the midtones apart leaves bright bundles with real gaps between them, and the low floor is what lets the gaps be gaps. */ float bundles = smoothstep(0.34, 0.86, rays); /* The curtain is a draped sheet, so it is bright where a fold turns edge on and nearly out where it faces us. A narrow range here is a band of even brightness, which is the other half of what made it read flat. */ float foldNoise = noise(vec2(q.x * 1.5 + f * 7.0, t * 0.25)); /* Bundles and folds are what a curtain is made many of, so both answer variance about their own midpoint: at 0 an even sheet, at 1 the clumping and the deep folds this was tuned to. */ float av = clamp(uVariance, 0.0, 1.0); float bundled = mix(mix(0.85, 0.1, av), mix(0.85, 1.6, av), bundles); float folded = mix(mix(0.775, 0.15, av), mix(0.775, 1.4, av), foldNoise); lit += edge * lengths * (rise * bundled * folded + rim) * (1.0 - f * 0.45); } return lit; } /* Light travelling in lanes, at speed. * * The one shape here that is about motion rather than about a form. Each lane * carries a trail with its own speed, length and phase, so the field reads as * something passing rather than something standing: the streaks the earlier * ground plane wanted and never got. * * The wrap is deliberately outside the frame. A trail restarting is a pop, so * the travel runs to plus and minus 1.8 while the visible field ends nearer * 1.2, and the reset happens where nobody is looking. * * The pointer is an obstacle: lanes bow around it and slow through it, the way * anything moving past a body does. Pushed outward in proportion to the offset * rather than by its sign, because a sign is a discontinuity and a * discontinuity in a displacement is a crease. */ float streaks(vec2 q, float t, vec2 qp, float reach) { float near = falloff(dot(q - qp, q - qp), 1.6) * reach; vec2 s = q + vec2((q.x - qp.x) * near * 1.1, 0.0); /* Three lanes are visited, not one, and that is the fix for a square edge. Each lane draws its speed, phase and length from a hash of its index, so every one of them is at a different point in its cycle. Sampled from the single lane a fragment falls in, the whole strip changes state at the boundary and the field acquires a hard vertical line at every lane edge: measured at 23 straight edges across the frame, and at a tilt of 90 the same count arrives horizontal, which is what says they belong to the shape's own axes rather than to the screen. Visiting the neighbours and weighting each by its own distance is the same answer particles already uses for the same reason. The weight reaches zero between centres, so nothing is left to step. */ /* **Fewer lanes, and not all of them carry anything.** At 2.4 a frame held a dozen streaks at once and read as rain: a streak is an event, and a field of simultaneous events is a texture. Sixteen hundredths of the lanes and a little over half of those alive puts the count at about two fifths of what it was. A dead lane contributes nothing anywhere rather than being cut off somewhere, so it costs the three lane blend nothing. */ float laneF = s.x * 1.6; float base = floor(laneF); float lit = 0.0; /* Three lanes, which is what the widths support. The tail spreads to at most 0.15 and lanes sit 0.417 apart, so one lane out carries about a fiftieth and the lane that drops out of the visited set, two out, is around a ten millionth. That dropped lane is where a step could appear, and it is the whole reason this loop is not a single lane. */ for (int k = -1; k <= 1; k++) { float id = base + float(k); float within = laneF - (id + 0.5); /* Speed and length were already drawn per lane, and measure a little over four times and seventy times across a frame. What was not drawn was width, which came out flat at 47 to 53 pixels on every lane, so a set that moved variously was still a set of identical objects. All four now scale from a common resting value, so a variance of 0 is a rank of equal streaks at one speed rather than a special case. Phase is never scaled: lanes sharing a phase march in lockstep, which is not a uniform population but a broken one. */ /* Clamped, and the upper half of that is not defensive tidying. These are mix() calls, so a value past 1 extrapolates rather than exaggerating: at 1.6 the length term reaches zero and beyond it goes negative, which makes exp(-behind / len) grow instead of decay and the lane becomes a full-height white bar. Measured at 2, the frame held 93 apparent lanes and six straight edges. There is nothing above 1 worth reaching, the resting spread already being fourfold in speed. */ float v = clamp(uVariance, 0.0, 1.0); float alive = step(0.42, hash(vec2(id, 97.0))); float speed = mix(1.3, 0.55 + hash(vec2(id, 11.0)) * 1.5, v); float phase = hash(vec2(id, 29.0)); /* Longer than they were. At 0.3 to 1.3 the tail was spent within about half the gap and each streak read as a blob with a smudge behind it; the thing is named for the trail, so the trail is the part that should dominate the head. */ /* Shorter than it was. A plume that stays bright for two and a half units is a searchlight: the frame is two units tall. */ float len = mix(0.85, 0.5 + hash(vec2(id, 47.0)) * 0.8, v); /* **The lane is periodic, not a single streak that is put back when it runs out.** It was fract() over a fixed span of 3.6, so a head left the top at 1.8 and was moved to -1.8, taking whatever of its tail was still on screen with it. That span is only off screen while the frame is small enough to sit inside it, and the visible half-extent is (|sin tilt| * aspect + |cos tilt|) * scale, which reaches 1.97 at a tilt of 45 and 2.0 at a scale of 2. Past that the removal happens in plain view, which is the popping. Making the field periodic in y removes the event rather than moving it out of sight: heads sit at every integer of u and the whole rank slides through, so there is no frame in which one is created or destroyed and no scale or tilt at which that becomes visible. P is the gap between successive heads in a lane, and it is what density is now made of. It varies too: lanes that are alike in spacing read as a grid however much else about them differs. */ /* Wider spacing, because the tails are longer: at the old gap a streak's tail reached the next one's nose and the lane read as a dashed line rather than as separate things travelling. */ float gap = mix(4.2, 3.2 + hash(vec2(id, 59.0)) * 2.2, v); float travel = phase + t * speed * 1.8 / gap; float u = s.y / gap - travel; float w = fract(u); /* **A streak is one solid, not a brightness curve times a fixed width.** Drawn separably it is a dart, and that is what these were: along the lane the light stopped over a fifth of a unit, across it the lane kept its full width the whole way, and the level sets of such a product meet at a point. Straight edges and an apex, which is a paper dart. So each term carries its own width. The tail leaves the head narrow and spreads as it falls behind, and the front is a round cap rather than a full-width wall cut off across the lane. Together that is a teardrop, which is the silhouette the thing actually has. */ float across = within / 1.6; /* 0.06, which is what the profile it replaces actually measured. Lanes sit 0.417 apart and the old exp(-|within| * 4) was half-height at 0.072 of a lane, so a sigma of 0.15 was two and a half times too wide: every lane overlapped both neighbours and the frame came out a blue wash with no streaks in it at all. */ /* Thinner, and paired with the longer tail below. Length against width is what makes a streak read as a streak: at a ratio near four these were stubby rods with rounded ends whichever way they tapered, and the fix for that is proportion rather than another change of profile. */ float wide = mix(0.045, 0.03 + hash(vec2(id, 71.0)) * 0.04, v); /* **A comet is a nucleus with a coma, and a plume behind it.** Neither of the two shapes this has been was that. A round cap the width of the body with the body widening behind it drew a bulb on a shaft; tapering the front instead drew a hairline that reads as a scratch. The fault common to both is that the head glow was computed from the distance *in front of* a head only, so there was never a round bright thing at the head at all, just where the profile happened to start. The glow is centred on the head now, measured to whichever head is nearer along the lane, so it is symmetric about the nucleus the way a coma is. */ float behind = (1.0 - w) * gap; float ahead = w * gap; float toHead = min(ahead, behind); float nose = wide * 0.5; float near2 = toHead * toHead + across * across; float nucleus = exp(-near2 / (2.0 * nose * nose)); float coma = exp(-near2 / (2.0 * (nose * 3.0) * (nose * 3.0))) * 0.42; /* The plume opens fast and fades fast, and is never as bright as the head. A tail that holds its brightness for its whole length is a streak of paint; what makes a comet read is that almost all of the light is in the first tenth of it. The onset is what keeps it continuous across a head. The plume exists only behind, so its value would step from nothing to something at the nucleus; ramping it in over a seventh of its own length puts that transition under the brightest part of the coma, where there is nothing left to see. */ float onset = 1.0 - exp(-behind / (0.15 * len)); /* **The straight edge was a min().** Clamping the plume's width with min(nose * (1 + behind * 3), 0.16) saturates at a constant value of behind, and a constant behind is a straight line across the lane: above it the width was fixed and below it grew, and the kink between the two drew a hard diagonal through the frame. A cap on a quantity that varies along one axis is a cap along a line, which is the one shape this thing must not have. A falloff this soft spans a few hundred 8-bit steps across a screen, and without a sub-step of noise it paints as visible rings. */ float dither = (hash(gl_FragCoord.xy) - 0.5) / 255.0; color = vec4(rgb + dither, 1.0); } `
declarations.description:
One program, branching on a uniform, for all five shapes.

A branch on a uniform is uniform across the whole draw, so every lane takes
the same path and it costs a jump rather than divergence. Five programs would
mean compiling and linking on a property change, which is the one moment a
reader is watching.

**No backticks anywhere inside this string, including in comments.** One ends
the template literal early, and what follows is parsed as JavaScript: it has
silently stripped every brace out of a shader and left the driver reporting a
syntax error two hundred lines from the cause. `bun run check:shaders` fails
the build on it.

They overlap by a step of space, which is enough to read as a stack without
the faces occluding each other. Each carries a ring in the page's own
background color, because a stack with no separation between its members
reads as one shape rather than several: the ring is what makes the edge of
each avatar visible against the one behind it.

Each avatar is drawn over the one before it, which falls out of document
order and needs no `z-index`. The familiar trick for putting the *first*
avatar on top is `row-reverse`, and it also reverses the row: the person
written first appears last. A facepile whose reading order is the reverse of
its markup is the worse trade of the two.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the columns are made of.

**A third axis on the chart, not on the bar.** A bar is a mark inside a
drawing and nobody writes markup for one; the chart is what a consumer
addresses, so the choice belongs here and reaches every column at once.

`glass` lets the gridlines read through the columns, which is what puts a
chart in the same language as a glass header rather than leaving it the one
opaque slab on the page.

**`gradient` was here and is `wash` now, which is #156.** The two set
different properties, `fill-opacity` against `fill`, and a chart forced into
both renders as a translucent gradient that is distinct from either: one
enum was holding two independent things, which is the mistake `Card`'s own
doc warns about arriving on the component that borrowed the word.

Absent is solid, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet describes only the departure. The strength is the
theme's: `glass` scales with `--helix-material-opacity`, so a language that
is more see-through everywhere is more see-through here.

Styled rather than headless, because what a bar is filled with is a
treatment and this tier is where treatments live. The gradient it points at
is drawn below, which is an element and therefore that tier's business.

members.name: wash
members.description:
How a column's fill is distributed across it.

`gradient` fades each column toward its base, into the wash the headless
tier draws whether or not anything points at it.

**A chart-domain axis and deliberately not a library one.** It lives on this
family alone, and here it is a way of encoding data rather than a way of
expressing a theme: promoted to the registry it would put an attribute on
eighty-eight components that means nothing on eighty-seven. `wash` because
that is what the tier below already calls it, in `--chart-bar-wash` and in
the `bar-wash-start` and `bar-wash-end` stops.

members.name: glass
members.description:
Which series are glass rather than solid, by name.

Matched the way `outlined` is, against the column headings the table gives.

**Per series for the reason `emphasis` is, arrived at one axis later.** A
chart-wide material puts every column in the same substance, which is right
when the whole chart is joining the page's language and wrong the moment one
series is a different kind of fact from the others. The two axes take the
same shape because they answer the same question about the same thing: what
is *this series* made of, and how much ink does *this series* claim.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the columns claim.

The chart's treatment, which every series takes unless `outlined` or
`subtle` names it. `outlined` is the mark as its edge alone, `subtle` a wash
of the series colour with that edge on it, and absent is the filled column,
per the rule that a reflected property takes no default.

**It composes with `material` rather than competing with it.** Emphasis
decides what is drawn and material decides how much of it comes through, so
`glass` thins whatever emphasis put there: the fill on a solid column, the
stroke on an outlined one. That corner was inert when the two were first
put side by side, `glass` setting a fill opacity on a mark whose fill is
`none`, and a combination that silently does nothing is the trap
`--card-backdrop` was for the one commit it shipped alone.

members.name: outlined
members.description:
Which series are drawn as an outline rather than a fill, by name.

Space separated and matched against the column headings the table gives,
the way `lines` and `secondary` are, so a chart says `outlined="Forecast"`
rather than counting columns. Names because they are what the table already
carries and what the legend already shows.

**The case this exists for is a series that is not a measurement.** A
forecast, a target, a budget: something drawn on the same axis as the
others and not the same kind of fact, which an outline says without a
second legend or a note under the chart.

Per series and not per bar, because a bar is a mark inside a drawing and
nobody writes markup for one, which is the same reason `material` sits on
the chart.

members.name: subtle
members.description: Which series are drawn as a wash of their colour, by name. Matched as `outlined` is.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: rows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: direction
members.description:
Whether the categories run down the side rather than along the bottom.

Absent is columns. `horizontal` is the one to reach for when the category
names are words rather than dates: a row of long names either overlaps or
turns on its side, and neither is as readable as putting them down the left
where they read normally.

members.name: gridlines
members.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none. `value` rules the axis the columns are *measured* on,
`category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on with one through each
group, and `both` draws both. Which of those is horizontal turns with
`direction`, because a rule belongs to an axis and not to a screen edge.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised: an
unrecognised value that draws nothing is indistinguishable from the
attribute being absent, which is the one thing a reader cannot debug.

`category` is the quieter half of this on a bar chart and is here for
completeness rather than because it is usually right: columns already
divide the categories by being separate columns, and a rule through each
one is a second statement of the same fact. It earns its place on a chart
of many thin bars, where the eye has stopped counting.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

members.name: lines
members.description:
Which series are drawn as a line instead of as columns, by name.

Space separated, matched against the column headings the table gives, so a
chart says `lines="Margin"` rather than counting columns. Names because
they are what the table already carries and what the legend already shows:
an index is a fourth place the column order is written down and the first
one to go stale when somebody moves a column.

**A combination chart is one scale, and that is the honest half of it.**
Both marks are measured against the same domain, so a line here says
something comparable to the columns beside it. The usual reason to reach
for a combination chart is the other thing, a count against a percentage on
a second axis, and that is deliberately not this: two scales on one frame
let the author put any two shapes in any relation by choosing the ranges,
and the reader has no way to see it happening.

A line among columns still measures from zero, because the columns do and
they share the axis. That is the trade for comparability, and it is why
this is a bar chart that can carry a line rather than a line chart that can
carry columns.

members.name: secondary
members.description:
Which series are measured against a scale of their own, by name.

Space separated and matched the way `lines` is, against the column headings
the table gives. Opt in: absent, every series shares one domain, which is
what makes a chart comparable and is the right default.

**Two scales on one frame let an author put any two shapes in any relation
by choosing the ranges, and a reader cannot see it happening.** That is not
a caveat, it is what the feature does: a line that crosses the columns
twice and a line that never touches them can be the same two series drawn
against different ranges. It earns its place when the two quantities are
genuinely incomparable, a count against a percentage, and it is a way to
mislead in every other case.

**So it draws its axes**, and that is not optional here. The chart renders
no value axis at all when there is one scale, because the columns are
measured against each other and a reader needs no numbers to do that. With
two, a reader has no way of knowing there are two, let alone which series
is on which, so both scales are labelled the moment this is set. An
unlabelled second axis is the deceptive case rather than the tidy one.

The grid stays on the primary axis, since a rule measured against two
scales at once is a rule that means nothing. The tooltip is unaffected: it
has always shown every column's own number, which is the reader's way out
of any scale question the picture raises.

members.name: lined
