members.name: renderPlot
members.description:
The columns themselves, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

`aria-hidden`, because the table it was read from is the readable version
and a screen reader hearing both hears the same numbers twice.

members.name: renderAxis
members.description:
The numbers along one scale, drawn only where there are two of them.

**A chart with one scale renders no axis, on purpose.** Columns measured
against each other need no numbers to be compared, and a row of them beside
a small chart is furniture that makes the drawing smaller for no reading a
reader was going to do. With two scales that argument inverts: a reader
cannot tell there are two, cannot tell which series is on which, and cannot
recover either from the picture. So this appears with `secondary` and never
without it.

**Beside the plot and not inside it**, which is the second thing this got
wrong. Inside, the numbers are drawn over the drawing, and a horizontal
chart shows it immediately: its value axis runs along the bottom, which is
where the last row of bars is. The vertical case has the same fault and
enough slack to hide it. The plot is also the pointer's catchment and the
tooltip's containing block, both measured from its box, so padding it to
make room would move every reading half an axis to the right.

A column of the host grid instead, which the stylesheet grows only when
`secondary` is set. That is what the property reflects for.

The primary hugs the edge the drawing starts at and the secondary the edge
it ends at: down the two sides for columns, along the bottom and top for
bars, which is where each axis is when the chart is turned.

members.name: renderGridlines
members.description:
The grid, behind everything, or nothing at all.

Across the measured axis, which turns with `direction`: a rule belongs to
the axis the bars are measured on and not the one they are arranged on, so
columns get horizontal rules and rows get vertical ones. Getting that
backwards draws a grid that divides the categories, which are already
divided by being separate bars.

Drawn before the baseline, so where a gridline and zero coincide the
baseline is what shows: zero is a fact about the data and a gridline is a
ruler.

members.name: renderBand
members.description:
The slot the pointer is resting in, drawn behind the columns.

**The honest version of the fade.** A group under the pointer already sets
`data-active` and the stylesheet dims the others, which says which group is
meant by making four of five quieter: it reads as the chart losing
confidence rather than as one column being pointed at. A band says the same
thing by lighting the region the pointer is actually in, and the region is
the whole slot, because that is the catchment the pointer resolves against.

Both are kept. The fade separates the active group from its neighbours and
the band says where the neighbourhood is, and on a chart of two categories
the fade alone is ambiguous about which half is lit.

members.name: renderLine
members.description:
One series drawn as a line across the categories, behind a seam.

Through the middle of each slot, which is where the group stands, so a
point sits over its own columns rather than over the gap between two of
them. The same arithmetic the category gridlines use, and for the same
reason: the reading is the thing, the boundary is only where the pointer
changes its mind.

`data-series` keeps the index the series has among *all* of them, not among
the lines, so the colour a line takes is the colour the legend gives it and
moving a column between marks does not repaint the chart.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
What a pointer resting on a reading shows.

A seam over `drawTooltip`, which holds the markup every chart shares. The
usual reason to override is arrangement: every cell of the row is already
there, including the columns nothing was plotted from.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: material
attributes.description:
What the columns are made of.

**A third axis on the chart, not on the bar.** A bar is a mark inside a
drawing and nobody writes markup for one; the chart is what a consumer
addresses, so the choice belongs here and reaches every column at once.

`glass` lets the gridlines read through the columns, which is what puts a
chart in the same language as a glass header rather than leaving it the one
opaque slab on the page.

**`gradient` was here and is `wash` now, which is #156.** The two set
different properties, `fill-opacity` against `fill`, and a chart forced into
both renders as a translucent gradient that is distinct from either: one
enum was holding two independent things, which is the mistake `Card`'s own
doc warns about arriving on the component that borrowed the word.

Absent is solid, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet describes only the departure. The strength is the
theme's: `glass` scales with `--helix-material-opacity`, so a language that
is more see-through everywhere is more see-through here.

Styled rather than headless, because what a bar is filled with is a
treatment and this tier is where treatments live. The gradient it points at
is drawn below, which is an element and therefore that tier's business.

attributes.name: wash
attributes.description:
How a column's fill is distributed across it.

`gradient` fades each column toward its base, into the wash the headless
tier draws whether or not anything points at it.

**A chart-domain axis and deliberately not a library one.** It lives on this
family alone, and here it is a way of encoding data rather than a way of
expressing a theme: promoted to the registry it would put an attribute on
eighty-eight components that means nothing on eighty-seven. `wash` because
that is what the tier below already calls it, in `--chart-bar-wash` and in
the `bar-wash-start` and `bar-wash-end` stops.

attributes.name: glass
attributes.description:
Which series are glass rather than solid, by name.

Matched the way `outlined` is, against the column headings the table gives.

**Per series for the reason `emphasis` is, arrived at one axis later.** A
chart-wide material puts every column in the same substance, which is right
when the whole chart is joining the page's language and wrong the moment one
series is a different kind of fact from the others. The two axes take the
same shape because they answer the same question about the same thing: what
is *this series* made of, and how much ink does *this series* claim.

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:
How much ink the columns claim.

The chart's treatment, which every series takes unless `outlined` or
`subtle` names it. `outlined` is the mark as its edge alone, `subtle` a wash
of the series colour with that edge on it, and absent is the filled column,
per the rule that a reflected property takes no default.

**It composes with `material` rather than competing with it.** Emphasis
decides what is drawn and material decides how much of it comes through, so
`glass` thins whatever emphasis put there: the fill on a solid column, the
stroke on an outlined one. That corner was inert when the two were first
put side by side, `glass` setting a fill opacity on a mark whose fill is
`none`, and a combination that silently does nothing is the trap
`--card-backdrop` was for the one commit it shipped alone.

attributes.name: outlined
attributes.description:
Which series are drawn as an outline rather than a fill, by name.

Space separated and matched against the column headings the table gives,
the way `lines` and `secondary` are, so a chart says `outlined="Forecast"`
rather than counting columns. Names because they are what the table already
carries and what the legend already shows.

**The case this exists for is a series that is not a measurement.** A
forecast, a target, a budget: something drawn on the same axis as the
others and not the same kind of fact, which an outline says without a
second legend or a note under the chart.

Per series and not per bar, because a bar is a mark inside a drawing and
nobody writes markup for one, which is the same reason `material` sits on
the chart.

attributes.name: subtle
attributes.description: Which series are drawn as a wash of their colour, by name. Matched as `outlined` is.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

attributes.name: direction
attributes.description:
Whether the categories run down the side rather than along the bottom.

Absent is columns. `horizontal` is the one to reach for when the category
names are words rather than dates: a row of long names either overlaps or
turns on its side, and neither is as readable as putting them down the left
where they read normally.

attributes.name: gridlines
attributes.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none. `value` rules the axis the columns are *measured* on,
`category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on with one through each
group, and `both` draws both. Which of those is horizontal turns with
`direction`, because a rule belongs to an axis and not to a screen edge.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised: an
unrecognised value that draws nothing is indistinguishable from the
attribute being absent, which is the one thing a reader cannot debug.

completeness rather than because it is usually right: columns already
divide the categories by being separate columns, and a rule through each
one is a second statement of the same fact. It earns its place on a chart
of many thin bars, where the eye has stopped counting.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

attributes.name: lines
attributes.description:
Which series are drawn as a line instead of as columns, by name.

Space separated, matched against the column headings the table gives, so a

they are what the table already carries and what the legend already shows:

one to go stale when somebody moves a column.

**A combination chart is one scale, and that is the honest half of it.**
Both marks are measured against the same domain, so a line here says
something comparable to the columns beside it. The usual reason to reach
for a combination chart is the other thing, a count against a percentage on
a second axis, and that is deliberately not this: two scales on one frame
let the author put any two shapes in any relation by choosing the ranges,
and the reader has no way to see it happening.

A line among columns still measures from zero, because the columns do and
they share the axis. That is the trade for comparability, and it is why
this is a bar chart that can carry a line rather than a line chart that can
carry columns.

attributes.name: secondary
attributes.description:
Which series are measured against a scale of their own, by name.

Space separated and matched the way `lines` is, against the column headings
the table gives. Opt in: absent, every series shares one domain, which is
what makes a chart comparable and is the right default.

**Two scales on one frame let an author put any two shapes in any relation

twice and a line that never touches them can be the same two series drawn

genuinely incomparable, a count against a percentage, and it is a way to
mislead in every other case.

**So it draws its axes**, and that is not optional here. The chart renders
no value axis at all when there is one scale, because the columns are
measured against each other and a reader needs no numbers to do that. With
two, a reader has no way of knowing there are two, let alone which series
is on which, so both scales are labelled the moment this is set. An
unlabelled second axis is the deceptive case rather than the tidy one.

The grid stays on the primary axis, since a rule measured against two
scales at once is a rule that means nothing. The tooltip is unaffected: it
has always shown every column's own number, which is the reader's way out
of any scale question the picture raises.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: width
members.description: How much of the space available to it the button takes. - `auto` is the default and is never written: the button is as wide as its label, which is what a control in a toolbar or beside a field should be. - `standard` is one width for every button that takes it, so a column or row of actions lines up instead of following the length of each word. - `full` fills the container, for a single action at the foot of a form or a card, and on a phone where a control is a target before it is a label. **This was `fill`, and the name had to disclaim itself.** The paragraph here opened "Width and not weight", which is a sentence a name should not need: `emphasis` on this same element is documented as "How filled it is drawn", so a button carried a property called `fill` beside a property about being filled, meaning different things. `separation="filled"` and `ThemeIntent.separation`'s `fill` mechanism both mean a surface's own colour, and every chart in the library writes `fill` for paint, which left this the only use of the word meaning geometry. `Dialog` had already made the same move for the same reason, its `appearance` becoming `size` for saying how wide a panel is, "which its own description admitted in as many words". `size` is not available here, because that rule's test is whether two of them sitting together could legitimately differ, and two buttons do: this is a width *policy* rather than a scale, and `standard` exists precisely to stop a row being ragged. Width and not weight, still. `emphasis` says how much a button matters and this says how much room it takes, and the three are independent: a `ghost standard` Cancel beside a `solid primary standard` Save is exactly the pairing a dialog wants. **A consumer's own anchor takes it as `data-button-width`**, the way it takes the emphasis as `data-button`: ```html Save ``` Both are one declaration in the base layer. They were not, and that was a real gap rather than a missing convenience: this class promises a link styled as a button and a real button are indistinguishable, and a dialog's button row is built on `standard`, so the one place the promise mattered most was the one place it did not hold.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the colour
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a colour of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where

attributes.name: name
attributes.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.description:
What kind of attention the passage needs.

**`severity` was a sixth spelling of `tone`**, which is the axis for what a
thing means, and a subset of it: a callout reports a status and never a
brand role, so it takes four of the seven. One word per axis is the whole
of the registry, and two words for one axis is how `tone` had drifted into
five incompatible value sets before anything held it.

members.description:
The mark for the callout's tone, behind a seam.

Slot fallback, so a consumer replaces it by slotting; and a method, so the
tier above replaces it by overriding. Those answer different people: the
slot is for the page and the method is for whoever is building the styled
layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

The mark and its label are passed in rather than looked up again, since
`render` has already resolved the tone and a second lookup is a second
place for the fallback to disagree with the tone around it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

`media` runs edge to edge and clips to the card's corners, so an image needs

members.name: separation
members.description:
How the card separates itself from the page.

**One value per mechanism, and the theme has the same four.**
`ThemeIntent.separation` is `border | fill | shadow | space`, so these are
the component's words for what a theme states as a policy, one to one. It
was `appearance`, which is the library's word for four different questions
and is being retired from all of them: `outlined` on a Card says where the
surface ends and `outlined` on a Button says how much ink, and one word
cannot keep saying both.

- `outlined` is the default, and a hairline is usually enough. It costs
  less attention than a shadow: a screen of shadowed cards reads as a stack
  of things floating, none of them settled.
- `elevated` is lifted off the page instead of framed, for a card on a
  colored or busy background, where a line has to compete with whatever is
  behind it and a shadow does not.
- `filled` is told apart by its own colour, with neither edge nor lift. For
  a dense surface where a border on every card is a grid of lines, and for
  a theme whose `separation` policy is `fill`, which pushes the surface
  ladder away from the page precisely so this reads.
- `plain` has no frame at all: the card is a layout and whatever it sits in
  is the surface. For a card inside something already bounded, where a
  second box adds a line and no meaning.

**`filled` is new and it closes a hole the engine could already see.**
`plain` clears the ground *and* the edge, so a surface with its own colour
and neither edge nor lift was unsayable while being one of the four things
a theme could ask for.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the card is made of.

**A third axis, and it passes the test the other two answer to.**
`separation` is where the surface ends and `tone` is what it means; both of
those can be true at once with this, an elevated glass card being a
perfectly ordinary thing to want, so it is not a value of either.

**An attribute rather than a hook, because glass is not one declaration.**
It is a translucent ground *and* a backdrop filter, and either without the
other does nothing: a blur behind an opaque background is invisible, and a
translucent card over an unfiltered page is a smear. `--card-backdrop`
shipped on its own for exactly one commit and was that trap, a published
hook a consumer could set and see nothing happen. The component owns the
pair; a theme owns how strong it is.

Absent is opaque, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet only describes the departure.

members.name: orientation
members.description: Whether media sits above the content stack or beside it.

members.name: mediaPlacement
members.description:
Puts the media after the content instead of before it.

**A figure that concludes a card is the same region as one that opens it**,
and the only thing that differs is which edge it is flush against. Media is
the one region that escapes the inset, so a chart wanting to span the card
has nowhere else to be: slotted into the content it keeps the padding on
both sides, and there is no second bleeding region to add without saying
twice what this says once.

Reflected and undefaulted, so a card that has not asked reads as a card
with no attribute on it and the stylesheet only describes the departure.

declarations.description:
The track scroll-snaps, so a drag and a trackpad swipe move it with the
browser's own momentum and the controls only have to scroll.

Slides take the full track by default. `per-view` fits more than one across,
up to five, and is declared on the tier below because it decides how many
positions the track has rather than only how wide a slide is,
which is what a run of cards wants rather than a run of full-width panels.
declarations.name: HelixCarousel

cssProperties.description: Height of a vertical track.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-block-size

cssProperties.description: Room inside the scroller so a slide's own shadow, border or focus ring is not clipped by it. Defaults to enough for `--helix-shadow-md`, which reaches 16px below the box it is on; a slide on `--helix-shadow-lg` reaches 44px and wants more.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-bleed

cssProperties.description: Space between slides.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-gap

members.name: indicatorPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the dots sit on.

Unset is `block-end`, under them. `block-start` puts them above,
`inline-start` and `inline-end` beside, where a run of dots becomes a
column.

**The sides of the content, not positions along a bar.** This was
`start | center | end`, which answered "where along the row" when the
question is "which edge", and could not say "above" at all. The logical
names rather than `top`/`left`, because the component is already careful
about writing direction everywhere else and an `inline-start` carousel
should put its dots on the right in Arabic without being told.

Independent of `controlsPlacement`. Both default to the block end, where
they share the row and split it, dots to the start and arrows to the end.
That is the arrangement the old shared bar gave, arrived at by two defaults
rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

members.name: indicatorAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

members.name: controlsPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

members.name: controlsAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the carousel.

members.name: index
members.description:
The slide in view, counted from zero.

Reading gives the real slide, in either mode. Writing sets it, the way a
script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an
`index` by then: declared, and the consumer owns it and the carousel only
announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

The same contract the four mixins carry, written out here rather than
extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the track runs.

Behavior rather than presentation, which is why it is here: the scroll
position and the nearest-slide arithmetic are both single-axis, and a
styled-tier attribute cannot change which one they read. Two sites branch
on it, `scrollTo` and the drag settle, and nothing else in the component
knows about the axis at all.

A vertical track needs a height, which a horizontal one does not: width
comes from the page and height does not, so the styled tier gives it
`--carousel-block-size` and a consumer sets that to whatever the slides
want.

members.name: defaultIndex
members.description: Slide to start on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: indexState
members.description: The slide in view, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: indexMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns the slide, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: loop
members.description: Whether moving past either end wraps to the other.

members.name: autoplay
members.description: Whether the carousel advances on its own.

members.name: interval
members.description: How long each slide is held, in milliseconds.

members.name: rotating
members.description: Whether rotation is running. Absent until autoplay starts it.

members.name: perView
members.description:
How many slides are shown across the track at once. Absent shows one.

**Here rather than on the styled tier, because it decides how many places
the track can stop.** It was declared above as a width, which is what it
looks like from the stylesheet: one rule per value setting a custom
property, and the slides divide the track by it. But a carousel showing
four of six slides has three positions, not six, and everything that counts
positions is in this file. Left up there, `goTo` clamped to the last
*slide*, so three of the six indicators pointed at a scroll offset the
track had already reached and could not pass: pressing next walked the dots
to the end while the slides stopped moving a third of the way through.

No default, because it reflects. A reflected property with a value writes
its attribute on upgrade, and the host then carries something a consumer's
server markup never had, which React reports as a mismatch. The one-across
case is the absent attribute, and the styles read it that way.

members.name: positions
members.description:
How many distinct views the track holds, which is what the indicators count.

A window of `perView` slides sliding one at a time over `n` of them stops
`n - perView + 1` times, so six slides four across is three: 0 to 3, 1 to 4,
2 to 5. One at minimum, since a carousel showing everything it has still
has the one place to be.

members.name: slides
members.description: The slides, in light-DOM order. Empty on the server, which has no tree.

members.name: handleIndicatorKeydown
members.description:
The arrows move between indicators, which is the tablist pattern.

One tab stop for the set and the arrows within it, so a reader does not
have to press Tab once per slide to get past a carousel of twelve. Moving
changes the slide, because an indicator that could be focused without
selecting would leave the highlight and the slide disagreeing with nothing
on screen saying which is which.

members.name: goTo
members.description: Moves to a slide, wrapping only where `loop` says to.

members.name: bleed
members.description:
The leading padding the track keeps for a slide to draw its own edge in.

A styled track carries one so a slide's shadow and focus ring have
somewhere to go: a scroll container clips at its padding box, and a slide
flush against that edge loses whatever it paints outside itself. The
headless tier has no stylesheet and so no padding, and this reads zero
there, which is why both tiers can share the arithmetic below.

Physical sides rather than logical, to match the physical `offsetLeft` and
`offsetTop` it is subtracted from. The bleed is one length on all four
sides, so the two agree whatever the writing mode; if that stops being
true, this is the method that has to know.

members.name: edgeOf
members.description:
Where a slide's leading edge sits, in the scroller's own coordinates.

**Both directions go through here, because they have to agree.** The
offsets are measured to the track's *border* box and `scrollTop` and
`scrollLeft` are measured from its content box, so the two differ by the
bleed: sending the carousel to a slide and reading back which slide it is
on used the same expression, and correcting one of them alone put a drag
one position off what the arrows did.

Unsubtracted, the leading slide's own offset *is* the bleed, so scrolling
to index 0 put its edge back on the clip edge. Measured on the insights
carousel: `scrollLeft` resting at 4 against a 4px bleed, the first card
shaved, and no scrolling done to cause it.

members.name: settling
members.description:
Whether the scroll now settling is one this component asked for.

Cleared by the first `scrollend` after it is set, and by a reader taking
hold of the track. The second half is not belt and braces: a `scrollTo`
whose target is already the scroll position fires no `scrollend` at all,
and the clamped end of a `per-view` track is exactly that case. Measured:
clicking past the last reachable slide moves `index` and produces no
`scrollend`, so a flag that only a `scrollend` could clear would stay set
and swallow the reader's next drag.

members.name: stop
members.description:
Stops rotation for good.

Hovering away or moving focus out does not start it again. The APG is
explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks for it, because a
carousel that starts moving again on its own is the thing the control
exists to escape.

members.name: runTimer
members.description:
Owns the timer, from the state rather than from the call site.

`start()` and `stop()` each held the interval and `connectedCallback`
started one, which the rules forbid: a DOM move re-ran connect and restarted
rotation the reader had stopped, and the server, which never runs connect at
all, rendered the control saying the opposite of what it would do. The
state is what is declared and the timer follows it, which also means one
place clears it.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
Reads where a reader's drag settled, and only a reader's.

**The scroll we issued ourselves ends with a `scrollend` too, and taking it
as a reading is what makes the dots jump back.** This ran on every one, so
the index a reader had just chosen was overwritten by whichever slide
happened to be nearest the leading edge at the moment the animation
finished. Any disagreement there is enough: a snap settling a pixel short of
a midpoint, a target clamped by the scroller's own maximum, a fractional
layout, or a smooth scroll cut off by the next click. The component asked
for slide four, the pixels said three, and the pixels won.

Which is the wrong precedence in one direction only. A drag is the reader
moving the track and the index has to follow it; a click is the reader
moving the index and the track has to follow *that*. One `scrollend` cannot
tell those apart, so the flag does.

members.name: stopped
members.description:
Whether the reader has stopped it, as opposed to something pausing it.

The two were one flag and the difference matters: `focusin` bubbles, so
every focus move inside the carousel re-ran `stop()`, and a reader who
pressed Start had it undone by their very next Tab. Pausing on hover and on
focus is right; forgetting that the reader asked it to stop is not, and the
APG is explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks.

members.name: pause
members.description: Pauses without forgetting that the reader wanted it running.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: indicator-placement
attributes.description:
Which side of the slides the dots sit on.

Unset is `block-end`, under them. `block-start` puts them above,
`inline-start` and `inline-end` beside, where a run of dots becomes a
column.

**The sides of the content, not positions along a bar.** This was
`start | center | end`, which answered "where along the row" when the
question is "which edge", and could not say "above" at all. The logical
names rather than `top`/`left`, because the component is already careful
about writing direction everywhere else and an `inline-start` carousel
should put its dots on the right in Arabic without being told.

Independent of `controlsPlacement`. Both default to the block end, where
they share the row and split it, dots to the start and arrows to the end.
That is the arrangement the old shared bar gave, arrived at by two defaults
rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

attributes.name: indicator-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

attributes.name: controls-placement
attributes.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

attributes.name: controls-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the carousel.

attributes.name: index
attributes.description:
The slide in view, counted from zero.

Reading gives the real slide, in either mode. Writing sets it, the way a
script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an
`index` by then: declared, and the consumer owns it and the carousel only
announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

The same contract the four mixins carry, written out here rather than
extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

attributes.name: orientation
attributes.description:
Which way the track runs.

Behavior rather than presentation, which is why it is here: the scroll
position and the nearest-slide arithmetic are both single-axis, and a
styled-tier attribute cannot change which one they read. Two sites branch
on it, `scrollTo` and the drag settle, and nothing else in the component
knows about the axis at all.

A vertical track needs a height, which a horizontal one does not: width
comes from the page and height does not, so the styled tier gives it
`--carousel-block-size` and a consumer sets that to whatever the slides
want.

attributes.name: default-index
attributes.description: Slide to start on, where nothing declared one.

attributes.name: loop
attributes.description: Whether moving past either end wraps to the other.

attributes.name: autoplay
attributes.description: Whether the carousel advances on its own.

attributes.name: interval
attributes.description: How long each slide is held, in milliseconds.

attributes.name: per-view
attributes.description:
How many slides are shown across the track at once. Absent shows one.

**Here rather than on the styled tier, because it decides how many places
the track can stop.** It was declared above as a width, which is what it
looks like from the stylesheet: one rule per value setting a custom
property, and the slides divide the track by it. But a carousel showing
four of six slides has three positions, not six, and everything that counts
positions is in this file. Left up there, `goTo` clamped to the last
*slide*, so three of the six indicators pointed at a scroll offset the
track had already reached and could not pass: pressing next walked the dots
to the end while the slides stopped moving a third of the way through.

No default, because it reflects. A reflected property with a value writes
its attribute on upgrade, and the host then carries something a consumer's
server markup never had, which React reports as a mismatch. The one-across
case is the absent attribute, and the styles read it that way.

members.name: orientation
members.description: Which way the boxes run.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: value
members.description: The checked values, comma separated.

members.name: boxes
members.description: The boxes, in light-DOM order. Client only: the server has no tree.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Pushes the group's name and value onto the boxes.

As properties rather than attributes. A `name` written onto a box is a
change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up. A box that names itself keeps its own.

members.name: seed
members.description:
Reads the boxes' own state into `value`, once, before anything is pushed.

`sync` used to refuse to write anything while `value` was empty, and the
guard was there for this: a group written with no `value` and boxes that
declare their own `checked` would have had them all cleared on the first
update. What it also did was make `group.value = ''` do nothing at all, so
the obvious way to clear a group silently did not, and the last box could
not be unticked through the group either.

Seeding is the honest version of the same intent. The markup decides the
starting set, exactly as before, and from then on `value` is what the boxes
follow, including when it is empty. The group's `value` is a derived read
of the boxes rather than state it owns, so reading it out of them at the
start is what it already means.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Reads a box's requested change into `value`, and says so once.

The box is found from the event's target, which does two things. It tells
the group which box asked, where the detail carries only the shared name.
And it ignores the group's own dispatch, which lands on this same listener
because the group is what it is dispatched from: without the guard the
group answers itself until the stack gives out.

The requested state comes from the event rather than from the box. Driving
the boxes from `value` makes them controlled, so a controlled box applies
nothing on its own and reports what it was asked for. Reading `checked`
here would read the state it still holds and nothing would ever change.

members.name: validate
members.description:
Refuses an empty set where one was required, which nothing did.

`required` arrives with `MixinField`, reflects, and paints the asterisk
through the composed field sheet, and enforced nothing at all: no validity,
no message, and nothing cascading to the boxes. A group marked required
submitted empty.

**The group is form-associated, and submits nothing.** It was not, on the
reasoning that its boxes are the controls and each submits itself, which is
still true: nothing here calls `setFormValue`, so the set that reaches the
server is exactly the boxes it always was. What form association buys is the
other half of participation, validity, and there is no other mechanism for
it: `setValidity` throws `NotSupportedError` on an element the platform does
not know is a control.

So the fix that was written for "a group marked required submitted empty"
threw on every update in a real browser, and happy-dom's shim does not
throw, so the specs passed and the behaviour never worked. Eleven of them
failed the moment they were run in Chromium. It is also what makes the rest
work: the form now refuses to submit, which fires `invalid`, which is what
marks the field touched and puts the message on screen.

Anchored on the list, because the browser needs somewhere to point the
bubble.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
