declarations.description:
The field is a box rather than a line, because nothing is typed into it: its
height is not a line of text, and what a reader aims at is the whole area. The
border is dashed for the same reason a drop target usually is, which is the
only affordance one has before anything is being dragged.

The native input is kept and laid over the field at zero opacity rather than
hidden, so a click anywhere on the box lands on the input itself and opens the
picker. Hiding it with `display: none` would take it out of the tab order and
out of the form, and a script clicking a hidden input is the same thing with
more moving parts.

The focus ring is drawn on the field, because the control it belongs to is
invisible.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: accept
members.description: Which files the picker offers, as a native `accept` list.

members.name: multiple
members.description: Whether more than one file can be chosen.

members.name: capture
members.description: Which camera or microphone a mobile picker should offer, if any.

members.name: triggerLabel
members.description: What the trigger reads, where nothing is slotted into it.

members.name: locale
members.description: Language tag the sizes are written in. Absent uses the runtime's own.

members.name: removeLabel
members.description: What the control removing one file is called, per file.

members.name: dropping
members.description:
Whether something is being dragged over the field.

State rather than a property: it is a fact about a gesture in progress and
nothing a consumer sets. It reaches the stylesheet as `data-dropping` on an
element in this shadow root, never on the host, which is markup a consumer
rendered.

members.name: files
members.description:
The files chosen, which is the element's own and never assigned.

Read from the input rather than mirrored into a field. The input is what
the picker filled and what a form submits, so a copy here could only ever
disagree with it.

members.name: control
members.description:
The input, or nothing where there is no tree to ask.

The guard is for the server, whose element shim carries attributes but not
traversal: `render` reads `files`, `files` reads this, and an unguarded
`querySelector` threw before a single character of markup came out. Nothing
is lost by answering `null` there, because a file only ever arrives through
a reader and a server has never met one.

members.name: clear
members.description:
Takes every file back out.

The one change a consumer can ask for. Setting a `FileList` is refused by
every browser for a reason worth keeping, but emptying one is not: nothing
about the page learns anything it did not already have.

members.name: removeAt
members.description:
Drops one file, by index.

`removeAt` rather than `remove`, which is `Element`'s own and takes no
arguments: shadowing it would break every caller who meant the node.

Through `DataTransfer`, which is the only way to build a `FileList`: the
type has no constructor and `input.files` takes nothing else. It is the same
mechanism a drop uses, so a file put in by dragging and one put in by the
picker come back out the same way.

members.name: announce
members.description: Says what is now chosen, by name, and puts it in the form.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Reports the files and the validity the host stands behind.

`FormData` rather than a string, because a file input submits the file
itself and several of them under one name. The anchor on `setValidity` is
the input, so the browser's own bubble points at something a reader can see
rather than at a host with no text in it.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts focus on the input, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description: Empties it, which is what a form reset means for a file input.

members.name: renderMeta
members.description:
What is known about a chosen file, as tags, behind a seam the styled tier
can move.

One method for both the size and the kind, because they are the same
element saying two things and two methods would be two places to keep in
step. Both parts are written out rather than passed in, and that is not
style: a part name behind an interpolation is a part the manifest cannot
see, so `check:selectors` reported the stylesheet as matching nothing the
moment this took the name as an argument.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own,
wrap this one, pass it a property the base does not know about, or leave it
out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The tag is
interpolated rather than written, so `tier` resolves it: this renders the
base element, and a styled subclass that sets `tier` renders the styled one
from the same template.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

The host is the flex container itself and the only child is a slot, so the
element adds no box of its own: `<helix-flex>` costs exactly the `<div>` it
replaces.

There is no separate Stack. A stack is this with `direction="column"`, and a
second element whose whole definition is one default of the first is a name
to learn rather than a capability to gain.

Gap takes a space token name rather than a length, so spacing stays on the
scale. A layout that can say `gap="13px"` is one that will.

Presentation only, so there is no headless tier: the split exists to keep
behavior separate from styling, and this is entirely styling.

members.name: applyTemplate
members.description:
Writes the track list into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, and the difference is
hydration. An inline style on the host is an attribute the element gives
itself once it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup does not have
it and hydration reports a mismatch it will not patch up. The shadow root
is not part of the tree React hydrates, so a rule written there is free.

The element is filled imperatively because Lit refuses expressions inside
`<style>`: it is an invalid binding location and throws while rendering
rather than at build time. Hence a static, empty element in the template
and its `textContent` set here.

It sets a custom property rather than the track list itself. A shadow
root's adopted stylesheets cascade *after* its own `<style>` elements, and
`static styles` is adopted, so a `grid-template-columns` here lost to the
one in the stylesheet and every `min` grid came out a single column. The
stylesheet only ever reads `--_grid-template`, so there is nothing to
lose against.

The consequence is that a server-rendered grid falls back to the
stylesheet's single column until it upgrades. That is why `columns` is also
expressed as plain CSS below: the fixed-count case, which can be enumerated,
needs no JavaScript at all, and only `min` depends on this.

members.name: shape
members.description:
The outline it is cut to, which is an axis of its own and not a value on one.

`emphasis` says how filled it is and `tone` says what it means; neither of
them says what shape it is, and folding a shape into either would put a
control's outline in the same word as its colour. A rounded square is the
resting one because that is what a control in a row of controls should be.

`circle` is the floating action button, and it is the reason this exists: a
round, raised, primary control holding the one action a screen is for. It is
a shape rather than a component, because a component would re-declare
`emphasis`, `tone`, `label` and the size around a control that already has
them, and because the same shape is wanted by an avatar's overlay, a media
control and a map's own buttons. Where it sits is the page's business: see
`data-dock` in the base layer.

members.name: raised
members.description:
Whether it is raised off the page it sits on.

Separate from `shape`, because they are separate facts: a docked control is
raised whatever its outline, and a circle inside a toolbar is not raised at
all. Shadow rather than a border, since what is under a floating control is
the page and a line drawn on the page is not the same as being above it.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the colour
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a colour of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: alt

Empty is a real answer and means decoration. Omitting the attribute is not
the same thing: a reader with nothing to read announces the file name.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether to wait until it is nearly on screen.

`lazy` by default, which is the opposite of the platform's, because a
picture worth putting in a component is usually below the fold and the one
that is not is the exception worth writing down.

members.name: srcset

members.name: fetchPriority
members.description:
How urgently to fetch it, for the one picture that is the page.

The hero of a page is usually its largest contentful paint, and the fix is
two attributes rather than one: `loading="eager"` stops it waiting for the
viewport, and this stops it queueing behind everything else the parser
found first. Left alone the browser decides, which is right for the other
ninety-nine pictures.

members.name: status
members.description:
Whether the picture is on its way, here, or never coming.

Read-only to a consumer: it is a report rather than a setting.

**Mirrored to `data-status`, and not reflected as `status`.** It is element
state, so reflecting it puts the element's own bookkeeping into the markup
a consumer rendered: React reads the attribute appearing at upgrade as a
hydration mismatch, and a serialized `<helix-image status="loaded">` pasted
back declares that a picture has arrived which this element has never
fetched. The `data-` name is the library's answer to both, being a
different name a re-parse cannot mistake for a declaration, and it is what
`data-open` and `data-checked` already do.

`loading` writes nothing, because it is where every image starts and the
resting state of a mirror is the attribute's absence.

members.name: answered
members.description: Which `src` the current status belongs to, so a new one starts over.

members.name: announce
members.description: Says so, because the platform's own saying of it cannot be heard. `load` and `error` on an `` neither bubble nor compose, so the ones fired inside this shadow root reach nobody outside it. A consumer had a reflected attribute and a `MutationObserver` and nothing else.

members.name: settle
members.description:
Catches the picture that was already there.

A cached image can finish loading before this element has a listener on it,
and then `load` never fires and the placeholder stays up over a picture that
is sitting right behind it. `complete` is the platform's own answer to that
question, and `naturalWidth` separates a decoded picture from one that
carries no pixels, which `complete` reports as finished either way.

**It can only ever conclude success.** A picture that has not been attempted
looks exactly like one that failed: `complete` is true and `naturalWidth` is
zero for both, and a DOM that never fetches anything reports that for every
image it has. Deciding `error` here called every picture broken the moment
it rendered. Failure has an event of its own and that event is reliable, so
this is only here to catch the success that happened too early to hear.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: placeholder
members.description: Shown while the field is empty. Not a label: it goes when typing starts.

members.name: readOnly
members.description: Whether the field refuses input while still submitting its value.

members.name: type
members.description:
What the field accepts, which decides the keyboard and the validation.

**Not reflected**, and it was. Reflection exists so a selector can reach a
value, and no stylesheet in this repository selects on `type`: what it did
instead was write `type="text"` onto every `<helix-input>` ever rendered,
an attribute no consumer's markup had. That is precisely the fault `Button`
had with `href`, `target` and `rel`, written up in the area rules as the
reason the rule exists, and this was the last property in the library still
doing it. Audited: ten reflected attributes have no selector anywhere, and
this is the only one of them with a value that puts itself on the host.

Nothing reads it from the attribute either. The real `<input>` inside takes
it as a property binding, which is what makes the keyboard and the
validation follow.

members.name: clearable
members.description:
Whether the field offers a button that empties it.

Shown only while there is something to clear, because a control that does
nothing is worse than no control: a reader who presses it and sees no
change has to work out whether the field was already empty or the button
is broken.

members.name: clearLabel
members.description: What the clear button is called, since an icon has no name of its own.

members.name: reveal
members.description:
Whether a password field offers a toggle that shows what was typed.

Ignored on every other type. A reveal on an email field would be a button
that does nothing visible, and guarding it here rather than asking the
consumer not to means the property can be set once on a component that
changes type.

members.name: revealLabel
members.description: What the reveal toggle is called. The state is `aria-pressed`, not this.

members.name: revealed
members.description:
Whether the password is currently showing.

State rather than a property: it is a reader's momentary choice about what
is on their own screen, it must not survive anything, and a consumer that
could set it could reveal a password without the reader asking.

members.name: effectiveType
members.description:
The type the real input is given, which is not always the type asked for.

A revealed password is a text field for exactly as long as the reader is
looking at it. Reading through a getter rather than mutating `type` keeps
the property the consumer's: what they set is what they get back, whatever
the button is doing.

members.name: showsClear
members.description: Whether there is a clear button on screen right now.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated to the input, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: handleInput
members.description:
Every keystroke, cancelable, and put back where it is refused.

The input has already taken the character by the time this runs, so a
consumer that refuses the change has to see the field returned to what the
element still holds. Otherwise the text on screen and the value the form
would submit disagree, which is the one thing a controlled field must never
do.

members.name: handleClear
members.description:
Empties the field and gives the caret back.

Focus returns to the input rather than staying on the button, which is
about to disappear: a reader who cleared a field is going to type in it,
and focus resting on a control that is being removed lands on the body.

Through `requestValue` like every other change, so a consumer who owns the
value hears about it and decides, and a cancelled clear leaves the text
where it was.

members.name: handleChange
members.description: Relayed, because `change` does not cross a shadow boundary on its own.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value and the validity the host stands behind.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the caret in the field, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: select
members.description: Selects everything in the field.

members.name: releaseCaret
members.description:
The caret, held across a value the consumer wrote rather than the reader.

Set in `willUpdate` and spent in `updated`, because Lit's `.value` binding
lands between the two and takes the selection with it. See `holdCaret`.

members.name: pattern
members.description:
A regular expression the value has to match, as the platform reads it.

The class documentation promised `pattern` and `minlength` "and the rest"
were set on the real input, and no such properties existed: a consumer
following that sentence wrote an attribute on the host, it reached no input,
and the field constrained nothing while looking as though it did.

Forwarded rather than checked here, which is the whole reason validity is
the platform's: the browser knows what a `pattern` means, anchors it at both
ends, and produces the message in the reader's own language.

members.name: minLength
members.description: Fewest characters the value may have.

members.name: maxLength
members.description: Most characters the value may have.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

attributes.name: default-value
attributes.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

attributes.name: hint
attributes.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

attributes.name: feedback
attributes.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

attributes.name: required
attributes.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

attributes.name: placeholder
attributes.description: Shown while the field is empty. Not a label: it goes when typing starts.

attributes.name: read-only
attributes.description: Whether the field refuses input while still submitting its value.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description:
What the field accepts, which decides the keyboard and the validation.

**Not reflected**, and it was. Reflection exists so a selector can reach a
value, and no stylesheet in this repository selects on `type`: what it did
instead was write `type="text"` onto every `<helix-input>` ever rendered,
an attribute no consumer's markup had. That is precisely the fault `Button`
had with `href`, `target` and `rel`, written up in the area rules as the
reason the rule exists, and this was the last property in the library still
doing it. Audited: ten reflected attributes have no selector anywhere, and
this is the only one of them with a value that puts itself on the host.

Nothing reads it from the attribute either. The real `<input>` inside takes
it as a property binding, which is what makes the keyboard and the
validation follow.

attributes.name: clearable
attributes.description:
Whether the field offers a button that empties it.

Shown only while there is something to clear, because a control that does
nothing is worse than no control: a reader who presses it and sees no
change has to work out whether the field was already empty or the button
is broken.

attributes.name: clear-label
attributes.description: What the clear button is called, since an icon has no name of its own.

attributes.name: reveal
attributes.description:
Whether a password field offers a toggle that shows what was typed.

Ignored on every other type. A reveal on an email field would be a button
that does nothing visible, and guarding it here rather than asking the
consumer not to means the property can be set once on a component that
changes type.

attributes.name: reveal-label
attributes.description: What the reveal toggle is called. The state is `aria-pressed`, not this.

attributes.name: pattern
attributes.description:
A regular expression the value has to match, as the platform reads it.

The class documentation promised `pattern` and `minlength` "and the rest"
were set on the real input, and no such properties existed: a consumer
following that sentence wrote an attribute on the host, it reached no input,
and the field constrained nothing while looking as though it did.

Forwarded rather than checked here, which is the whole reason validity is
the platform's: the browser knows what a `pattern` means, anchors it at both
ends, and produces the message in the reader's own language.

attributes.name: minlength
attributes.description: Fewest characters the value may have.

attributes.name: maxlength
attributes.description: Most characters the value may have.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

attributes.name: name
attributes.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: placement
members.description:
Where the legend sits and which way its entries run.

Absent is a wrapping row, which is what sits under a chart. `start` and
`end` stack the entries in a column, for a legend beside one.

**This says which way the entries run and not where the element is**, which
is the honest limit of a component that is a sibling of the chart rather
than part of it. A legend cannot place itself relative to something it is
not inside, so the consumer still puts it above, below or beside; this
makes it lay out correctly once it is there, which was the part that
previously took a custom property nobody would guess at.

The alternative was a `legend` slot on every chart, so a chart could place
its own. That is worse: it makes the legend's position a fact about the
chart, so two charts sharing one legend becomes impossible, and it puts a
list inside a drawing that is `aria-hidden`.

members.name: entries
members.description:
Which way to read the table.

Absent is `series`, one entry per data column. `categories` reads one entry
per body row instead, for a donut, whose slices are the rows.

members.name: for
members.description:

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a legend inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

The lines take the series palette in order, so a chart of one is series one
and a chart of four is the first four, and a legend beside it maps the same
twenty-four.

The stroke does not scale with the box. `preserveAspectRatio="none"` is what
lets one drawing fill a narrow card and a wide panel, and without

first and heavy in the second. It rescues strokes and not geometry, which is
why the readings are joined by lines and marked by nothing: a circle in a
stretched coordinate space is an ellipse, and there is no vector-effect that
answers for a shape.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: rows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: area
members.description:
Whether a wash is drawn under each line.

Absent is lines alone, which is what suits more than one series: washes
stack and the lower ones are read through the upper. One series over a
ground it should feel like a quantity against is the case for this.

members.name: curve
members.description:
How the line gets from one reading to the next.

**`smooth` is the resting curve.** *Changed 21 Aug 2026, reversing the
argument this comment used to make.* Joining the readings claims nothing in
between, which is true and is why `straight` still exists: a straight
segment asserts nothing about the values between two readings, and a curve
invents them. What settles it the other way is that the invention is
bounded. The interpolation is monotone cubic, so it never leaves the band
the data sets and never introduces a peak or a trough the series does not
have, and within that bound the smoothed line is the easier one to follow
across a long series. `straight` becomes the deliberate claim.

**Still absent rather than defaulted on the property**, because a
reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host
anybody renders, including the ones nobody configured.
`line-chart-root.ssr.spec.ts` asserts the host carries only what the
consumer wrote, and caught that the first time. The default therefore lives
where the path is built, as `curve ?? 'smooth'`.

`step` claims the opposite of both, that a reading holds until the next.

members.name: gridlines
members.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none, which is the honest default rather than a timid one: a
chart in a card and a chart beside a figure are read as a shape, and a grid
over one is furniture around a drawing nobody is measuring.

`value` rules the axis the readings are *measured* on, at the levels
`ticks` picks, which are round numbers anchored to the number line rather
than to where the data starts, so two charts over different ranges rule at
the same levels. `category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on, one
through each reading, which is what lets a point be traced down to its
label across a wide chart. `both` draws both.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised.
Written out, the attribute a consumer reaches for first should be the grid
they meant, and a typo should fall back to the useful half rather than to
nothing at all: an unrecognised value that draws no rules is
indistinguishable from the attribute being absent, which is the one thing
a reader cannot debug.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

members.name: rulesValue
members.description: Whether the levels are ruled, which is every value but `category`.

members.name: rulesCategory
members.description: Whether each reading is ruled, which only two values ask for.

members.name: zero
members.description:
Whether zero is forced into the range.

Absent measures from the data's own extent, which is what a line is for.
Set it where the distance from nothing is the point rather than the shape,
and accept that a series which never approaches zero becomes a flat rule
near the top of the box.

members.name: range
members.description: The domain every series is drawn against, which the tooltip also needs.

members.name: renderPlot
members.description:
The lines themselves, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

`aria-hidden`, because the table it was read from is the readable version
and a screen reader hearing both hears the same numbers twice.

members.name: renderGridlines
members.description:
The grid, behind everything, or nothing at all.

Drawn first so a series is never cut by a rule, and before the baseline so
that where the two coincide the baseline wins: zero is a fact about the
data and a gridline is a ruler, and the reader should see the fact.

members.name: renderBand
members.description:
The slot the pointer is resting in, drawn behind the drawing.

A band and not a second rule. The guide says exactly where the reading is
and the band says which share of the width belongs to it, which is what a
reader is actually pointing at: the catchment is a slot wide, so a pointer
a few pixels off the line is still asking about that reading, and without
the band nothing on screen says so.

The same slot arithmetic the pointer controller resolves with, so the lit
region and the region that answers are the same region by construction
rather than by two files agreeing.

members.name: renderGuide
members.description:
A rule down the reading the tooltip is about.

Without it the tooltip is a box of numbers floating over a drawing, and a
reader has to match its heading against the row of names to find out which
column it means. The rule is the whole of what connects the two, and it
matters most on a line, where there is no marker under the pointer to
stand in for one.

Drawn before the series so a line is never cut by it.

members.name: renderSeries
members.description: One series, its wash first so the line is drawn over its own fill.

members.name: renderLabels
members.description:
The reading names, as HTML beside the drawing rather than inside it.

Inside, they would scale with the box, for the reason the class doc gives.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
What a pointer resting on a reading shows.

A seam over `drawTooltip`, which holds the markup every chart shares. The
usual reason to override is arrangement: every cell of the row is already

declarations.summary: A series over time as a line, read from a table.

examples.description: Sessions a month, read from the table beside it. The cell text is what a reader sees and data-value is the number.
A wash under the line, for one series read as a quantity rather than a shape.
The same line chart on the headless tier, with every rule written by hand.
The three curves over one series: joined, smoothed, and held until the next reading.
Open incidents, where the distance from none is the reading: its own range turns a quiet year into a collapse.
Two series on one scale, with a legend mapping the same palette.
The same chart given different numbers, moving to the new shape rather than snapping to it.
A pointer resting on a reading, showing the whole row including a column nothing plotted.
Rules at the levels a reader would infer, so a reading can be placed against one.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

attributes.name: area
attributes.description:
Whether a wash is drawn under each line.

Absent is lines alone, which is what suits more than one series: washes
stack and the lower ones are read through the upper. One series over a
ground it should feel like a quantity against is the case for this.

attributes.name: curve
attributes.description:
How the line gets from one reading to the next.

**`smooth` is the resting curve.** *Changed 21 Aug 2026, reversing the
argument this comment used to make.* Joining the readings claims nothing in
between, which is true and is why `straight` still exists: a straight
segment asserts nothing about the values between two readings, and a curve
invents them. What settles it the other way is that the invention is
bounded. The interpolation is monotone cubic, so it never leaves the band
the data sets and never introduces a peak or a trough the series does not
have, and within that bound the smoothed line is the easier one to follow
across a long series. `straight` becomes the deliberate claim.

**Still absent rather than defaulted on the property**, because a
reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host
anybody renders, including the ones nobody configured.
`line-chart-root.ssr.spec.ts` asserts the host carries only what the
consumer wrote, and caught that the first time. The default therefore lives
where the path is built, as `curve ?? 'smooth'`.

`step` claims the opposite of both, that a reading holds until the next.

attributes.name: gridlines
attributes.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none, which is the honest default rather than a timid one: a
chart in a card and a chart beside a figure are read as a shape, and a grid
over one is furniture around a drawing nobody is measuring.

`value` rules the axis the readings are *measured* on, at the levels
`ticks` picks, which are round numbers anchored to the number line rather
than to where the data starts, so two charts over different ranges rule at
the same levels. `category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on, one
through each reading, which is what lets a point be traced down to its
label across a wide chart. `both` draws both.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised.
Written out, the attribute a consumer reaches for first should be the grid
they meant, and a typo should fall back to the useful half rather than to
nothing at all: an unrecognised value that draws no rules is
indistinguishable from the attribute being absent, which is the one thing
a reader cannot debug.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

attributes.name: zero
attributes.description:
Whether zero is forced into the range.

Absent measures from the data's own extent, which is what a line is for.
Set it where the distance from nothing is the point rather than the shape,
and accept that a series which never approaches zero becomes a flat rule
near the top of the box.

members.name: kind
members.description:
What kind of list this is, which is a fact about the content.

On the headless tier because it is meaning rather than decoration, the same
argument `severity` makes on `Callout`. A numbered list is numbered because
the order carries information; a bulleted one is bulleted because the items
are a set and the order does not. That distinction is the reader's, and it
has to survive with the stylesheet turned off.

- `default` is a run of rows and takes no marker. It is what a list of
  settings or files is: neither ordered nor a set to be counted.
- `ordered` numbers them, for steps.
- `unordered` bullets them, for a set.
- `description` pairs each row's label with its supporting text as a term
  and what the term means.

**`description` reuses the row's existing slots rather than inventing a
  second kind of row.** A term and its description is exactly the label and
  the supporting text `List.Item` already has, so the kind changes how the
  pair is drawn and nothing about what a consumer writes. A separate
  `List.Term` element would be a second row shape for one attribute's sake.
