members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: counted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: rows
members.description: How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: filter
members.description:
What the list is narrowed to, if anything.

Filtering hides rather than removes, so nothing about the value changes and
the list is still the consumer's own elements in their own order. Reading
gives what is being filtered on; writing declares it theirs, and
`default-filter` seeds one the list owns.

members.name: defaultFilter
members.description: What to start narrowed to, where nothing declared it.

members.name: filterState
members.description: What the list is narrowed to, whoever set it.

members.name: filterMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns the narrowing, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: filterable
members.description:
Whether the list renders a field for narrowing itself.

The field lives here rather than in whatever frames the list, because the
filtering already does: `filter`, the empty state and the keyboard are all
this component's. A select that drew its own search box above a listbox
would be writing the same field again, and so would a combobox, and so
would a command palette, which is the fault the three-family split exists
to prevent.

members.name: filterLabel
members.description: Placeholder for the field that narrows the list.

members.name: multiple
members.description: Whether more than one option can be the answer.

members.name: activeValue
members.description: Which option the keyboard is on, which is not what is chosen.

members.name: forwarded
members.description:
Whether the key being handled was forwarded rather than typed into this.

Plain state rather than reactive: it is set and cleared inside one
synchronous call, so nothing renders while it is true and nothing outside
can observe it.

members.name: hasMatches
members.description:
Whether anything survived the filter, kept as state rather than counted at
render time.

Counting during render reads the hiding from the *previous* pass, because
hiding happens in `updated` against options that are the consumer's
elements rather than this component's markup. So a filter matching nothing
rendered the full list, hid every option, and left an empty box with no
message in it: the count was right one pass too late. Written to state
instead, which schedules the one further render that shows it.

members.name: options
members.description:
Every option, in the order a reader meets them.

Descendants rather than children, because a group puts a level between the
list and its options and the keyboard has to move through a grouped list
exactly as it moves through a flat one.

members.name: collect
members.description:
Walks the tree, and walks *through* a slot when it meets one.

Descendants rather than children, because a group puts a level between the
list and its options and the keyboard has to move through a grouped list
exactly as it moves through a flat one.

Through a slot because that is how this gets composed. `Select` renders a
listbox in its own shadow root with a slot inside it, so the options are
the *select's* light DOM and the listbox's only child is the slot: a plain
`querySelectorAll` finds the slot and no options at all, and the whole
component comes up empty. Found the first time the two were put together,
which is the argument for building the pieces separately rather than
discovering it inside a finished Select.

members.name: groups
members.description: The groups, found the same way and for the same reason.

members.name: shown
members.description: The options a filter has left showing.

members.name: values
members.description: The chosen values, which is a list whether or not `multiple` is set.

members.name: choose
members.description:
Applies a choice, announcing first so a listener can refuse it.

With `multiple` a choice is a toggle, because the same press has to be able
to take an answer back; without it a choice replaces whatever was there.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Moves the keyboard, and chooses with it only where that is the pattern.

Space and Enter are how a multi-select list chooses, and they are also how
a single-select one confirms what the arrows already did, so they act
either way rather than being guarded on `multiple`.

members.name: navigate
members.description:
Runs the list's own key handling for a caller whose focus is elsewhere.

A combobox keeps focus in its text field, because that is the whole of what
a combobox is, and still has to move this list with the arrows. Without
this it would have to reimplement the moving, the wrapping, the skipping of
disabled options and the seeding from the current value, and the second
copy would drift from this one the first time either changed.

Public and taking the event rather than a direction, so a caller forwards
what it received and this decides what the key means. `preventDefault` is
called in here on the keys it acts on, so a caller can hand over every
keydown and let the list ignore the ones that are not its business.

The entry point is also what says whether moving chooses, which is why the
flag is set here rather than exposed as a property. The difference between
a listbox and a combobox is not a mode a consumer picks: it is which
element the reader's focus is in, and that is exactly what calling this
rather than being typed into means. Enter and Space still choose, because
those are the caller asking for the answer rather than for a move.

members.name: reveal
members.description:
Brings the chosen option to rest in the middle of the list.

A method rather than something this does on its own, because a listbox
opening on its answer usually wants it merely *visible* and the browser
already manages that: centring is what a caller wants when the list is being
read as a dial rather than scanned as a list, which is what Time Picker's wheels
does with three of these.

A delta from the two boxes rather than `offsetTop`. An option is a slotted
light DOM child, so its `offsetParent` is whatever is positioned above it,
which is not this list and is not guaranteed to be anything: measuring both
rects and moving by the difference needs no such assumption.

members.name: place
members.description: Hides what the filter excludes, and writes the rest onto the options.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: currentValue
members.description:
Where the reader is, and failing that where the answer is.

`activeValue` starts empty, so the first arrow press in a list that already
has a chosen option started from nowhere: Down went to the first option,
which is a move backwards from anything below it, and Up went to the last.
Seeding from the value means the first press moves from what the reader can
see is selected.

**The keyboard knew this and the announcement did not.** `linkActive` asked
for `activeValue` alone, so a list that had been given a value and not yet
arrowed through pointed `aria-activedescendant` at nothing: a screen reader
was told the list and its selection, and nothing about where the cursor
was, until a key moved it. Both read this now, so the thing announced and
the thing the arrows move from cannot disagree.

members.name: handleFilter
members.description:
Narrows the list as the reader types, announcing it first.

`helix-filter` and not `helix-change`, because nothing about the value
changes: the options are hidden rather than removed, and telling a consumer
their answer moved when it did not is worse than telling them nothing. It
told them nothing before this.

members.name: requestFilter
members.description: Requests a narrowing, and reports whether the request stood.

members.name: handleFilterKeydown
members.description:
Sends the keys that belong to the list to the list.

A reader filtering is still choosing: they type two letters and press Down
to reach what is left, and the field would otherwise swallow it because the
arrows move a caret. Typing keys stay with the field, which is what makes
this different from forwarding everything.

Escape clears rather than closing. What frames the list may close on Escape
too, so this stops the event when there is something to clear: one press
empties the filter, a second reaches whatever is above and closes it. A
filter that closed the panel would lose the reader's place for a keystroke
they meant as an undo.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Focusing the host focuses the list inside it.

The focusable node is `[part="items"]`, a div in this shadow root, and a
caller outside has no way to reach it: `select` opened its panel and called
`.focus()` on this element, which is not focusable, so focus stayed on the
trigger and the arrow keys never reached the options at all. Delegation is
the platform answering that, and it keeps `document.activeElement` on the
host, which is what a caller reasons about.

members.name: renderFilterIcon
members.description:
The mark in the filter's field, behind a seam.

Slot fallback, so a consumer replaces it by slotting; and a method, so the
tier above replaces it by overriding. Those answer different people: the
slot is for the page and the method is for whoever is building the styled
layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: variant
members.description:
How the waiting is drawn.

Unset is the turning arc, which is what most waits want and what this
component was called for years.

`pulse` takes the arc away and lets the middle carry the motion on its own:
the ring stays as the quiet outline and swells, and whatever is slotted
swells with it, in step. It is the shape for a wait that has a mark to
show, a splash or a first paint behind a wordmark, where a rotating rim
around a logo reads as chrome bolted to the brand.

That the component can now be drawn without anything spinning is why it is
no longer called Spinner: the old name described one appearance of two.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: label
members.description: The section's name, which names the default trigger and the panel.

members.name: variant
members.description:
Whether the panel is a card under the trigger or a band across the page.

The resting one is the card, hanging off the trigger and as wide as it
needs to be. `full` is the other shape navigations use: a band from edge to
edge under the header, with its contents held to the page's own measure, so
a set of destinations too wide to sit under one word gets the whole width
to lay out in.

It changes where the panel goes as well as how it looks, which is why this
tier knows about it at all: a band spans the viewport, so there is nothing
to measure it against and nothing to flip or shift to, and the placing pass
is told not to run. Everything else the popover gives, the top layer and
the dismissal, is exactly what such a band needs.

members.name: openOn
members.description:
Whether hovering the trigger opens the panel, or only a press does.

A press always works. This says whether a mouse also opens it by resting on
the trigger, and it is the default because that is what a navigation bar
does. `click` is for a trigger that does something else as well, or a panel
heavy enough that opening it on the way past is rude.

members.name: fullBelow
members.description:
The width, in pixels, under which a card becomes a band. Zero never does.

A card is a panel hung off one word, and there is no room to hang anything
off a word on a phone: the columns do not shrink past
`--megamenu-column-size`, so four of them stay four of them and the panel
runs off the side of the screen rather than reflowing. Below this it takes
the whole width and its columns stack, which is the only arrangement that
fits.

**In script rather than a media query, and only once.** Whether the panel is
a band is not a question of paint: a band is not placed against the trigger,
so the controller has to be told not to measure, and that decision is here
whatever the stylesheet says. Writing the width in both places would be one
number in two languages, drifting the first time either moved. This sets
`data-narrow` on the host and the stylesheet arranges itself off that.

members.name: banded
members.description: A band, whether because it was asked for or because there is no room.

members.name: panel
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, /* The host, not the panel. A press on the trigger is a press on this element, and counting it as outside would close the panel on the way to the click that toggles it. `Menu` says the same about its own. */ boundary: () => this, onDismiss: () => this.close(), place: () => !this.banded, placement: () => 'bottom-start', surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="panel"]'), })

members.name: slotted
members.description: What the consumer slotted, if they slotted anything.

members.name: trigger
members.description: Whatever the consumer slotted, or the button rendered in its place.

members.name: close
members.description: Shuts it and puts the reader back where they were.

members.name: band
members.description:
Where a full-bleed band starts, which is the only number it needs.

The placing pass is off for that appearance, so nothing else is measuring:
a band spans the viewport and has only one degree of freedom, how far down
it sits, and that is the bottom of the trigger in viewport coordinates
because the panel is fixed. A header that scrolls takes the band with it,
which is what a panel hanging off a header should do.

Written as a custom property rather than an inline `top`, so the stylesheet
keeps the arrangement and this contributes the one measurement it cannot
make. Nothing to do for the card, which the controller places.

members.name: bar
members.description:
The bottom edge of the bar this hangs from.

The trigger's own bottom is the obvious answer and is the wrong one: a
header is taller than the word inside it, so a band starting at the word
starts partway up the header, over its lower padding and its border.
Measured: trigger bottom 44, header bottom 57, thirteen pixels of header
with a band drawn across it.

**The first ancestor as wide as the window, which is a fact and not a tag
name.** A band spans the viewport, so what it should hang from is whatever
else does: that is what makes something a bar. Asking for `helix-app-header`
by name would make this element know about that one, which is the coupling
`Menu` is careful not to have with `Drilldown`, and would leave a consumer
who wrote their own header with a band across it.

`body` ends the walk. It is as wide as the window and is not a bar, and its
bottom is the foot of the page: without the guard a megamenu on a plain page
would put its band down there. Nothing found means nothing to hang from, and
the trigger is the honest answer again.

members.name: OPEN_DELAY
members.description:
How long a pointer has to mean it, in milliseconds.

Opening is the shorter wait: too long and the panel feels stuck, too short
and crossing the bar opens things. Closing is longer because the pointer
has to get from the trigger to the panel, and the straight line between
them is not the line anybody moves along.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
Keeps a band under its bar while the page moves, and closes it when the bar
goes.

The band is fixed and its offset is measured once, when it opens. That is
fine until the page scrolls: a header that scrolls away leaves the band
pinned where the header used to be, open, in the middle of the page with
nothing above it. Measured at a scroll of 300: header bottom at -243 and the
band still sitting at 57.

The card has none of this, because the floating controller follows its
anchor. Turning that off for the band, which has nothing to be placed
against, took the scroll handling with it, and this is the half that was
still wanted.

A sticky bar does not move, so re-measuring returns the same number and the
band stays where it is. `requestOpen` rather than `close`, because closing
puts focus back on the trigger and a reader who has scrolled away should not
be dragged back up to it.

members.name: handleContentClick
members.description:
Shuts the panel when a reader takes one of the destinations in it.

Nothing closed it before, so a click navigated and left the panel hanging
over wherever the reader landed. With a router that navigates in place, and
this is one, that is a panel covering the page it was asked to go to.

**A modified click leaves it open**, which is the same position this
element already takes on middle clicks and the status bar: `cmd` on a link
opens a tab behind this page rather than navigating it, so the reader is
still standing in the menu and collecting, and shutting it under them would
make the second choice cost a second open.

`requestOpen(false)` rather than `close()`, for the reason `pointerleave`
gives: the trigger is not where the reader is going, and pulling focus back
to a nav bar they have just left is a scroll they did not ask for.

**On the host rather than on the panel**, which is the same reason the
pointer handlers give and one more. A row is slotted light DOM and the
panel is in the shadow root, so a click only reaches the panel through the
flattened tree: real ones do, and a DOM that does not implement slot
propagation never delivers it, which makes every case here pass by never
running this at all. The host is the row's own ancestor in both.

members.name: renderTrigger
members.description:
The control that opens it, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

The same case `SpeedDial` records: a bare `<button>` is what this tier can
write, `helix-button` lives a tier above, and a render method is how a tier
that has one reaches this without reimplementing the panel below it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: value
members.description: What this row stands for, carried in the event when it is chosen.

members.name: checkable
members.description:
Whether the row is one of a set of choices.

Separate from `checked`, and it has to be. A row that is off is still a
choice, and `checked` alone cannot say so: an unticked row and a row that
was never tickable look identical from here. Announcing only the ticked one
as a checkbox tells a reader its siblings are commands, which is the one
thing they are not.

`checked` implies it, so a row that is on never has to say both.

members.name: checked
members.description: Whether the row is ticked.

members.name: disabled
members.description: Whether the row can be chosen.

members.name: href
members.description:
Where the row goes, which makes it a real link.

**The row itself becomes an `<a>`, and the role goes with it.** A
`menuitem` cannot contain a link: measured in Chromium, an anchor inside
one is exposed as a child and the row loses its accessible name entirely.
So the anchor *is* the row, carrying `menuitem` and the `tabindex` the menu
roves, which is the same manoeuvre `Tree.Item` makes and the reason `href`
changes the markup rather than only adding an attribute.

**`Option` cannot have this and the reason is worth knowing**, since a
command palette is the obvious place to want it. A listbox has to keep
focus somewhere else, in the text field for a combobox, so it says which
option is current with `aria-activedescendant`. That reference can only
point at the option's host, measured: assigning
`ariaActiveDescendantElement` an element inside a sibling shadow root reads
back `null`. So `role="option"` is pinned to the host, and an anchor under
it hits the naming failure above. A menu has no such constraint because
focus really moves to the row.

members.name: target
members.description: Where the link opens, for the rows that should leave the page.

members.name: rel
members.description: The relationship, which `target="_blank"` should always set.

members.name: download
members.description:
Whether the link saves the file rather than opening it.

Only meaningful beside an `href`, and only for a file served from this
origin: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, which is the browser's rule
about who may name a file on somebody's disk rather than a gap here.

members.name: onPage
members.description:
Whether this row is on the page currently showing.

Set by the menu, and a property rather than an attribute for that reason.
Public because the menu has to reach it, and not something a consumer
writes: which page is open is the menu's business.

members.name: showingSubmenu
members.description:
Whether this row's submenu is the page showing.

Separate from `onPage`, and it has to be. A row that opened a page is not
itself on that page, so both are false for it, and rendering nothing on
that basis takes its `slot[name="submenu"]` with it: the rows inside have
nowhere to be assigned and are never laid out. The element that holds the
page has to keep the slot even when it shows no row of its own.

members.name: hasSubmenu
members.description:
Whether anything was slotted into `submenu`.

Client only, and the `?? []` is what makes that true rather than merely
documented. Lit's element shim carries attributes but not a tree, so
`children` is undefined on the server, and this getter is read during
`render`: spreading it threw, and a menu row could not be served at all.
Found by writing this component's SSR spec, which is the only place it
could have been found, because every other path runs in a browser.

False on the server is also the right answer rather than a safe one: the
server cannot know whether a submenu was slotted, and a row that served a
`aria-haspopup` it might not have would be a promise made to a screen
reader on the strength of a guess.

members.name: submenu
members.description:
Whether anything is slotted into `submenu`. Read after first render.

State rather than a getter over `children`, which is what it was: read
during `render()` with nothing to re-read it, a submenu arriving after the
row's first render produced no caret and no `aria-haspopup` while selecting
the row still drilled in. A framework filling a submenu on demand hit that
every time. `Tree.Item` backs `branch` the same way for the same reason.

Kept in step by `readSubmenu`, which is bound in the template rather than
once at first render. See the note there: bound once, a single drill-in left
it false for good.

False on the server is the right answer rather than a safe one: the server
cannot know whether a submenu was slotted, and a row that served an
`aria-haspopup` it might not have would be a promise made to a screen
reader on the strength of a guess.

members.name: readSubmenu
members.description:
Re-reads whether anything is in the submenu, from whichever slot is current.

**Bound in the template, and it has to be.** It was `addEventListener` on
the slot found at `firstUpdated`, which is a different element from the one
showing a moment later: this row renders a `slot[name="submenu"]` in two
template branches, one for the row and one for the page it opens, and moving
between them makes Lit build a new slot and throw the old one away. The
listener stayed on the discarded slot, and the discarded slot fired
`slotchange` on its way out with nothing assigned to it any more. So one
drill-in set `submenu` false and nothing was left listening to set it back:
every caret in the menu vanished and every row stopped opening. Reported
from a recording of the sandbox's Environment menu.

The live slot is asked rather than `event.target`, so it does not matter
which of the two fired or in what order.

members.name: focus
members.description:
Moves focus onto the row itself.

The host is not focusable: what takes focus is the row inside this shadow
root, and a menu moving between rows with the arrow keys has to reach it.

members.name: focusItem
members.description:
`NavigableItem`, so the arrow keys can be the shared controller's business.

`focus()` above already puts focus on the control inside the row rather than
on the row, which is the whole of what moving here means.

members.name: select
members.description: Chooses the row, which is the same act as pressing it.

members.name: selected
members.description:
Whether this is the row the set is on, which in a menu is where focus is.

A radio group's selection is an answer it holds; a menu has no answer, only
a row the reader has walked to, so focus is the whole of what "the current
one" can mean here. Read from the shadow root rather than kept as state,
because focus moves for reasons this element is not told about: a press, a
Tab, the drilldown putting the reader on the first row of a page it has
just opened.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Enter and Space choose the row, which a `<div>` would not do on its own.

It is not a `<button>`: a button inside a menu is announced as a button,
and the roles a menu needs are not roles a button can take.

**A linked row hands Enter back to the browser.** An anchor answers Enter
itself, by firing a click and following the link, so preventing the default
here would mean re-issuing that navigation by hand and losing whatever the
browser does around it. `Tree.Item` records the same trap from the other
side: its tree prevents every key it handles, which is exactly what was
swallowing Enter on its rows.

Space is different, and that is the platform rather than a choice: an
anchor ignores it. So the row presses itself, and the click that comes back
both announces and navigates.

Whether the row is one of a set of choices.

Separate from `checked`, and it has to be. A row that is off is still a
choice, and `checked` alone cannot say so: an unticked row and a row that
was never tickable look identical from here. Announcing only the ticked one
as a checkbox tells a reader its siblings are commands, which is the one
thing they are not.

`checked` implies it, so a row that is on never has to say both.

attributes.name: checked
attributes.description: Whether the row is ticked.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description: Whether the row can be chosen.

attributes.name: href
attributes.description:
Where the row goes, which makes it a real link.

**The row itself becomes an `<a>`, and the role goes with it.** A
`menuitem` cannot contain a link: measured in Chromium, an anchor inside
one is exposed as a child and the row loses its accessible name entirely.
So the anchor *is* the row, carrying `menuitem` and the `tabindex` the menu
roves, which is the same manoeuvre `Tree.Item` makes and the reason `href`
changes the markup rather than only adding an attribute.

**`Option` cannot have this and the reason is worth knowing**, since a
command palette is the obvious place to want it. A listbox has to keep
focus somewhere else, in the text field for a combobox, so it says which
option is current with `aria-activedescendant`. That reference can only
point at the option's host, measured: assigning
`ariaActiveDescendantElement` an element inside a sibling shadow root reads
back `null`. So `role="option"` is pinned to the host, and an anchor under
it hits the naming failure above. A menu has no such constraint because
focus really moves to the row.

attributes.name: target
attributes.description: Where the link opens, for the rows that should leave the page.

attributes.name: rel
attributes.description: The relationship, which `target="_blank"` should always set.

attributes.name: download
attributes.description:
Whether the link saves the file rather than opening it.

Only meaningful beside an `href`, and only for a file served from this
origin: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, which is the browser's rule
about who may name a file on somebody's disk rather than a gap here.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: counted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: rows
members.description: How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: placement
members.description: Preferred side. It moves if that side does not fit.

members.name: offset
members.description: Space between the trigger and the surface, in pixels.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the surface.

members.name: backLabel
members.description: What the row returning from a submenu reads.

members.name: drilldown
members.default: new DrilldownController<HelixBaseMenuItem>(this, { isRow: (element: Element): boolean => 'isMenuItem' in element && element.isMenuItem === true, root: () => [...this.children].filter((child) => child.slot !== 'trigger'), slot: 'submenu', })
members.description:
Which page is showing, and what is on it.

This was a `page` field, a title getter and an items getter written here.
None of them were about menus: a settings panel or a navigation tree wants
the same thing, and could not have it without being a menu. The controller
holds the same shape, so the port is a rename rather than a rewrite, and it
adds a real stack: `back()` returns one level instead of to the root, which
this could not do because it only ever went two deep.

members.name: keys
members.default: new KeyboardNavigationController(this, { items: () => this.items, reserved: () => ['ArrowLeft', 'ArrowRight'], selects: () => false, })
members.description:
Moving between rows, which is not this element's own business any more.

`selects` false, because arriving at Delete must not delete: moving and
choosing are one act in a radio group and two acts here, which is the
distinction the controller was already drawing for `Tabs`.

The origin is the selection, which took a wrong turn first and is worth
recording. `focus` looks like the right reading, since a menu's current row
is the focused one, but that origin also carries a rule a menu must not
follow: a press that did not come from the set moves nothing. That rule is
there for a tab panel, which is a tab stop beside the tabs; a menu's panel
holds the rows and nothing else, and Down on a menu that has just opened is
how a reader gets to the first row at all. It moved nothing, and the specs
written alongside this are what said so.

The horizontal pair is reserved rather than released. Right opens a
submenu and left comes back, which are the platform's own bindings for a
menu that drills, so those keys are spoken for here rather than unhandled.

members.name: panel
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, // The host is `display: contents`, so it has no box a press can land in. // What counts as inside is the surface, plus the trigger, whose own click // handler decides what a press there means. boundary: () => this, offset: () => this.offset, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="menu"]'), })

members.name: trigger
members.description: The element the surface opens against.

members.name: items
members.description: The items on the page that is showing, which is what the keys move over.

members.name: show
members.description: Opens the menu.

members.name: hide
members.description: Closes the menu, and forgets which page was showing.

members.name: enter
members.description: Shows an item's submenu in place of the current page.

members.name: leave
members.description: Returns to the page above, or closes when there is none.

members.name: handleFocusIn
members.description:
Keeps whatever has focus in sight, however it got there.

This was done in the arrow branches, which meant it was true of the arrow
keys and of nothing else: a row reached by Tab, or focused by the drilldown
on the way into a page, could sit below the fold of a scrolled panel. On
`focusin` it is one rule about focus rather than a line repeated in every
branch that moves it, and it survived the arrow keys moving out to a shared
controller that knows nothing about this panel.

members.name: mark
members.description:
Walks the tree marking which rows are on the page showing.

Two levels were marked by hand and nothing wrote `showingSubmenu` on a
nested row, so drilling into a third-level submenu rendered the header over
an empty panel: the page existed, its rows were still marked as belonging
to the level above, and none of them rendered. `Drilldown.mark()` is the
same walk and was already recursive.

`slot === 'submenu'` rather than every child, because a row's other
children are its label and its icons.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component

declarations.description:
The bar `Progress` draws, at twice the height and on the house corner rather
than its pill.

It shipped at the progress height, on the argument that the two stand beside
each other in a panel. Rendered side by side that turned out backwards: they
*are* two unrelated controls, and a reader telling a level from a task at a
glance is the point rather than the cost. A meter also carries more, a fill
and a mark at each threshold, and at eight pixels those marks are hairlines.
At sixteen they are unmistakable.

The corner is the ticks' doing: they cut the fill into segments, and a
pill-ended bar comes out as a run whose outer ends are round and whose inner
ends are square. `radii-full` on an eight pixel bar was a four pixel pill
anyway, so this is only a change at all because the bar grew.

What else differs is what the color means. A progress bar is one color because
there is one thing to say; a meter's fill takes the success, warning or danger
tone from the band its reading falls in, and only once thresholds have been
declared. An unbanded meter is neutral, because a gauge with nothing said
about it is a reading rather than good news.

A tick marks each threshold, so the reading can be placed against the bands
without seeing color at all.

A reading past either end squares the corner it ran out at, which is the
convention for a quantity continuing past the frame it is drawn in. The bar
itself stops, because that is what an end is; the words and the accessible
reading are what say how far past.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the reading.

members.name: min
members.description: Bottom of the range.

members.name: max
members.description:
Top of the range.

A hundred rather than the platform's one, which is what `Progress` already
takes and what a consumer writing `value="72"` means. A range of zero to one
is a fraction, and a component that reads `value="72"` as seventy-two times
over its maximum is a trap that costs nothing to avoid.

members.name: value
members.description: Where the reading sits between `min` and `max`. Outside them, it clamps.

members.name: low
members.description: Top of the low band. Absent leaves the range unbanded.

members.name: high
members.description: Bottom of the high band. Absent leaves the range unbanded.

members.name: optimum
members.description:
Where in the range it is best to be.

Defaults to the middle of whatever bands are declared, which is the
platform's own default and the right one for a score. A meter where low is
good, like disk usage, says `optimum="0"`; one where high is good, like a
battery, says `optimum="100"`.

members.name: band
members.description:
The band, said outright, where the three thresholds cannot say it.

**The specification's model has a shape, and it is worth knowing before
reaching for this.** Three bands and a point mean it can express a
*direction* in three grades, or a *target* in two, and never a target in
three. Measured across a grid: with `low="25" high="50" optimum="0"` the
readings 5, 28 and 60 come out good, fair and poor; with `low="15"
high="25" optimum="20"` the readings 28 and 90 both come out fair, because
from a middle band nothing is ever two bands away.

So a target you can miss badly in either direction has no expression in
`low`, `high` and `optimum`, and neither has a rule that is not about
distance at all: 28 against a target of 20 is fine for a room's temperature
and is not fine for a dosage, and no arrangement of thresholds knows which
one it is looking at.

Written, this wins outright and the thresholds are only for drawing the
ticks. A consumer whose rule is more than three buckets already knows the
answer, and asking them to encode it as thresholds so this can decode it
again is a worse API than letting them say it.

Not reflected. Nothing selects on it: the band reaches the stylesheet as
`data-band` on the fill, because that is the element being colored, so
reflecting here would write an attribute onto the host for no reader. Third
time this rule has caught something today.

members.name: shape
members.description:
Whether the reading is drawn as a bar, a ring or an arc.

A gauge and a meter are the same thing measured: a value in a range, with
bands saying which part of it is the good part. What differs between the two
words in practice is the drawing, so this is a shape rather than a second
component, the same call `Progress` made with its ring and `Skeleton` with
its own shapes.

A bar is right in a row of them, in a table, or under a label. A ring is
right in a tile, where the number goes in the middle. An arc is the shape a
dashboard gauge has always had: open at the bottom, so the two ends of the
range have somewhere to be that is not each other.

There is no needle in any of them. A needle is a picture of an instrument
rather than a reading, it costs a rotation and a shape to draw it with, and
it says nothing the end of the arc does not already say.

members.name: showValue
members.description: Whether the reading is shown beside the bar.

members.name: valueText
members.description:
What the reading says, where a number is not the whole story.

`value-text="18 GB of 32 GB"` is announced and shown instead of `56%`. The
same property `Progress` carries, for the same reason: a percentage is a
fair summary of a task and a poor one of a quantity.

members.name: span
members.description: The range, clamped so `max` is never at or below `min`.

members.name: reading
members.description: The reading, pulled into the range.

members.name: fraction
members.description:
How much of the track is filled, from zero to one.

Clamped, because a bar cannot draw past its own end. What the reading *says*
is not clamped: see `ratio`.

members.name: ratio
members.description:
Where the value really sits, which is what the words report.

**A value past the end used to be swallowed twice.** The bar filled and the
reading said "100%", so 110 and 250 were indistinguishable from exactly
full, measured. A meter that cannot say "you are over" is worse than no
meter for the one case anybody checks it in, and it is the same fault as a
pagination reporting a page it is not on: the number shown and the number
given disagree, quietly.

The bar still stops at its end, because that is what an end is. The words
and the accessible reading carry the truth, and `data-over` is on the fill
so a consumer can say more about it.

members.name: beyond
members.description: Whether the value is past an end, which the bar itself cannot show.

members.name: thresholds
members.description:
The thresholds, in order, or nothing where the consumer declared none.

Both are clamped into the range and to each other, because a `low` above a
`high` describes no bands at all and the spec's own answer is to raise the
one that is out of order rather than to give up.

members.name: computedBand
members.description:
Which band the reading is in, by the specification's rule.

`optimum` names a point, and the band containing it is the good one. A
reading in that band is good, one in a band beside it is fair, and one two
bands away is poor. Undefined where nothing was declared, which is what
keeps an unbanded meter from being painted as good news.

members.name: text
members.description: What the reading says, which is the consumer's words or a percentage.

members.name: renderRound
members.description:
The same reading, drawn round.

`pathLength="100"` is what makes every number here a percentage: the path is
declared a hundred units long, so nothing computes a circumference, a radius
or pi, and a consumer changing the thickness moves the circle that carries
it without this element recalculating anything. Progress does the same and
for the same reason.

The sweep is what separates the two shapes. A ring is the whole circle and
an arc is three quarters of it, open at the bottom, which is where a gauge
has always had its gap: the two ends need somewhere to be that is not each
other, and the opening is where a reading of the value goes.

Ticks are segments of the same circle rather than marks placed on it. One
unit of a hundred, offset to where the threshold falls, which needs no
trigonometry and stays correct at any radius or thickness. Placing them by
hand would mean sine and cosine in a template and a second definition of
where the arc starts.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.
