members.name: separation
members.description:
How the panel separates itself from what it floats over.

One of the axis's four values, which is all this surface has meaning for: a
floating panel keeps its lift by default, `ThemeIntent.separation.floating`
refusing `space` for the reason it refuses it everywhere, that a panel over
content nobody can predict has to be readable.

Unset is a surface with an inset, which is what a panel of content wants.
`plain` removes both, for a panel holding something that brings its own,
such as a list whose rows run to the edges.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, /* The host, not the panel. `display: contents` leaves it without a box, so a press on the trigger is inside the host and outside the panel, and a boundary of the panel alone would close on the very press that opened it. */ /* The host *and* whatever invoked it. An outside press is measured against this, and a `--toggle` button outside the host is part of the control by any reading a reader would give it: pressing it while the panel is open should close it once, not close it on `pointerdown` and reopen it on the `click` that follows. */ boundary: (): (HTMLElement | undefined)[] => [this, this.invoker], offset: () => this.offset, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="popover"]'), })

members.name: invoker
members.description:
The invoker that last opened the panel, when a command did.

The handlers discarded the `source` the controller hands them, which cost
two things at once. The panel was positioned against the host, and the
styled tier makes the host a boxless `display: contents` element, so a
popover opened by a command outside it opened against the window origin.
And the outside-press dismissal had no way to know the invoker was part of
the control: the press fires on `pointerdown`, the command arrives on the
`click` after it, so a `--toggle` button outside the host closed the panel
and immediately reopened it, for ever.

members.name: commands
members.default: new CommandController(this, { commands: { '--close': () => this.hide(), '--show': (source: Element | null) => { this.invoker = source instanceof HTMLElement ? source : undefined this.show() }, '--toggle': (source: Element | null) => { this.invoker = source instanceof HTMLElement ? source : undefined if (this.open) { this.hide() } else { this.show() } }, }, })

members.description:

On the headless tier rather than as a treatment, because it is
semantics before it is a picture: a progressbar with no `aria-valuenow` is
how the platform says "running, and nobody knows how far", and a reader on
a screen reader is told that rather than being read a number that means
nothing. `value` and `max` are ignored while it is set.

Not `Loader`, which is the other thing this could be. A loader says the
page is busy; a bar says a named piece of work is running, and keeps its
place in the layout when the answer arrives and it becomes determinate.

members.name: shape
members.description:

**On this tier because it changes the markup**, which is the base tier's to
own. A bar is two boxes and a ring is an SVG with two circles in it, and no
stylesheet turns one into the other: the styled tier tried, with a conic
gradient and a mask, and the thing it could not do was the round end the
loader has, because a gradient has hard radial edges and no notion of a
cap. `Skeleton.shape` is the same word for the same kind of decision.

The value, the ARIA and the form participation are untouched by it. What
changes is only which shape carries the fraction.

members.description:

a control that holds a number can either show it or leave it to whatever is
around it. Off by default, since most bars sit under a label that already
says what is happening and a second number is noise.

Nothing under `indeterminate`, where there is no reading to show: a percent
that does not move is worse than none, and `valueText` is the property for
saying "uploading" while the bar runs.

members.name: value
members.description:

Clamped between zero and `max` for both the fill and the announcement, so
the two can never disagree about what is on screen.

"3 of 8 files" rather than "37". Announced instead of the percentage, and
never instead of the value itself: `aria-valuenow` still carries the
number, because assistive technology that ignores the text still has to
report progress.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for what is in progress.

attributes.name: indeterminate
attributes.description:
Whether the work has a knowable end.

On the headless tier rather than as a treatment, because it is
semantics before it is a picture: a progressbar with no `aria-valuenow` is
how the platform says "running, and nobody knows how far", and a reader on
a screen reader is told that rather than being read a number that means
nothing. `value` and `max` are ignored while it is set.

Not `Loader`, which is the other thing this could be. A loader says the
page is busy; a bar says a named piece of work is running, and keeps its
place in the layout when the answer arrives and it becomes determinate.

attributes.name: max
attributes.description: The total the work is measured against.

attributes.name: shape
attributes.description:
Whether the value is drawn as a bar or as a ring.

**On this tier because it changes the markup**, which is the base tier's to
own. A bar is two boxes and a ring is an SVG with two circles in it, and no
stylesheet turns one into the other: the styled tier tried, with a conic
gradient and a mask, and the thing it could not do was the round end the
loader has, because a gradient has hard radial edges and no notion of a
cap. `Skeleton.shape` is the same word for the same kind of decision.

The value, the ARIA and the form participation are untouched by it. What
changes is only which shape carries the fraction.

attributes.name: show-value
attributes.description:
Whether the reading is shown beside the bar.

The same name and shape `Slider` uses, because it is the same question:
a control that holds a number can either show it or leave it to whatever is
around it. Off by default, since most bars sit under a label that already
says what is happening and a second number is noise.

Nothing under `indeterminate`, where there is no reading to show: a percent
that does not move is worse than none, and `valueText` is the property for
saying "uploading" while the bar runs.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What has been done so far, in the same units as `max`.

Clamped between zero and `max` for both the fill and the announcement, so
the two can never disagree about what is on screen.

attributes.name: value-text
attributes.description:
A reading for the value, where the number alone does not say enough.

"3 of 8 files" rather than "37". Announced instead of the percentage, and
never instead of the value itself: `aria-valuenow` still carries the
number, because assistive technology that ignores the text still has to
report progress.

declarations.description:

dark on light to read, and the pair that guarantees it is not the page's
foreground and background: those invert together in dark mode, and a code
drawn light-on-dark is refused by a good half of the scanners in the world.
So the ground is stated and the ink is the foreground it is chosen for.

members.name: value
members.description: What the code encodes, which is usually a URL.

members.name: label
members.description:
What the image is called.

Falling back to the value is deliberate: a code almost always holds a URL,
and a URL is a better name than "QR code" for a reader who cannot see it.

members.name: shape
members.description:
How the modules are drawn.

`square` is the default and the only one that joins runs of adjacent
modules into a single subpath, which is what keeps a thousand modules to a
handful of nodes. `rounded` and `dots` draw each module on its own, because
the corners are the thing being drawn and a joined run has none in the
middle. That cost is paid only by a code that asks for them.

A scanner reads contrast between cells, not their shape, so all three
scan. `dots` sits a little under half a module so neighbours do not touch,
which is what makes it read as dots rather than as a softened square code.

members.name: correction
members.description:
How much of the code can be lost and still read.

`M` by default, which is the level almost every code in the world uses and
costs about fifteen percent redundancy. `H` where a mark covers the centre,
chosen automatically when the slot is filled: it is the level that makes
covering safe, and a consumer who fills the slot has said what they want
without having to know that.

members.name: logo
members.description: Whether anything is slotted into the middle.

members.name: level
members.description: The level actually used, which the slot can raise.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

The field's three parts, laid out the way every other field lays them out: a
question over the set, and one line under it that is help until something is

declarations.name: HelixRadioGroup

cssProperties.description: Space between the choices.
cssProperties.name: --radio-group-gap

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the choices run. A column reads one line per answer.

**Optional rather than defaulted, which is not a style preference.** A
reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host the
moment the element upgrades, including the ones a consumer rendered and did
not touch, and React reads that as a hydration mismatch. The absent
attribute *is* the column, which the stylesheet reads as the base rule, so
only `horizontal` has to be named.

members.name: items
members.description: The radios, in light-DOM order. Client only: the server has no tree.

members.name: handleSelection
members.description:
Announces before it applies, so a listener can refuse the change.

The item has not moved by the time this runs, unlike a native input, so
refusing is simply not writing the value: there is nothing to put back.

members.name: place
members.description: Writes the answer onto the items, and nothing onto the host.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

members.name: tier
members.description:

`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says

own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the

subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:

source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per

members.description:

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: variant
members.description:
How the choice presents itself.

- `plain` is the default and is never written: a circle beside its words,
  which is what a list of choices should be almost always.
- `card` puts it in a bounded surface, for options that need room to
  explain themselves: a description, an icon, a price. It is the half a
  `data-card` link cannot do, because a link reports no value and belongs
  to no group, so a card that is genuinely an answer has to be this.

The circle stays in both. A card whose only marker was its own border would
ask a reader to compare surfaces across a row to find the answer, and would
leave nothing for a high-contrast display.

members.name: hideControl
members.description:
Takes the circle away, leaving the card as the whole control.

Unnecessary under `chip`, which has no room for a circle beside its mark
and hides it already.

`card` only, and it is a graphic that goes rather than a radio: the control
in the shadow root is untouched, so the row is still focusable, still
reported to a screen reader, and still the thing a form submits.

Safe because the card already carries the answer in its surface, a raised
fill inside a primary edge and a three-pixel ring of it. That ring is
recent, and before it there was nothing left saying which card was chosen,
which is why this is a property now and could not have been one then.

Not on `Checkbox`, deliberately. A radio card with no circle is still
unmistakably one-of-many because its siblings behave that way; a checkbox
card with no box loses the only thing that says you may pick several.

members.name: variant
members.description:
Which mark the row is drawn with.

`marks` is the star, and is what a rating means to most readers. `dots`
drops the glyph for a plain circle, which says how much rather than how
good: a star carries a judgement that a level of spice, a difficulty or a
confidence has not earned.

Both are one shape repeated and clipped to the score, so halves work in
either, and both are only a choice of drawing. A scale whose marks are
*different* drawings is a set of choices rather than a quantity: that is
`Radio.Group`, whose options already carry a value and a name each.

**Undefaulted, because it reflects.** Defaulted to `marks` it wrote
`appearance="marks"` onto every rating the server rendered, which React
held no prop for and reported as a hydration mismatch. The stylesheet was
already written the right way round, naming only `dots`, so marks is what
an unset one draws and nothing else had to move.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: max
members.description: How many marks there are.

members.name: step
members.description:
The smallest part of a mark that can be chosen.

`0.5` is the half star, and it is the reason the value is a number rather
than an index: with halves, five marks are ten answers.

members.name: readOnly
members.description:
Whether this shows a score rather than asks for one.

A readout is not a control that has been switched off. It takes no focus,
answers no keys, and reads as one thing: see the note on the class.

members.name: valueText
members.description:
How the score is read out, where "3.5 out of 5" is not what it should say.

A rating out of five is one of the few places a screen reader gets a worse
answer from the value than from a sentence: "3.5" alone is a number without
a subject. This names the readout, where a control is named by its `label`
and each of its options by the score that option is.

members.name: showValue
members.description:
Whether the score is written out beside the marks.

Marks say roughly, and a number says exactly. Four and a bit stars is not a
reading anyone can repeat, which is why a product's average is nearly always
printed next to them. `Meter` spells its reading the same way and under the
same attribute.

It follows the pointer, because it labels what the marks are showing rather
than what the form holds: a label that disagreed with the marks under the
reader's own cursor would be worse than no label.

members.name: markSource
members.description:
The shape a consumer slotted, if they slotted one.

Read rather than projected. A `<slot>` shows its content once and a rating
needs the shape as many times as there are marks, twice over because there
are two layers, so the slot here is a way of being handed the shape rather
than a place the shape is drawn. What is handed over gets cloned into every
position.

**One shape, not one per position.** A rating is a quantity of identical
marks and the fill is a clip across all of them, so a row whose third mark
is a different drawing from its first is not a rating: it is a set of
choices, which is `Radio.Group` and already carries a value and a name on
each of its own options. Anything past the first slotted element is
ignored.

members.name: previewing
members.description: What the pointer is over, which is shown instead of the score while it is.

members.name: keys

things and a `<button>` in a shadow root can answer all five without being

members.description: The pointer drawing a score, while one is.

members.name: clones
members.description:
One clone per place a mark goes, kept so a render does not remake them.

A drag renders on every pointer move, and handing Lit a fresh node each
time would swap every mark in the row on every frame of a gesture whose
whole point is that only the fill moves.

members.name: markFor
members.description: The shape for one place, or nothing when the stylesheet is drawing it.

members.name: scoreAt
members.description:
The step under a point on the row, or the nearest one to it.

Asked of the boxes rather than worked out from `max` and `step`, because
where a step sits is the stylesheet's arithmetic and this would be a second
copy of it that could disagree. The browser has already laid the targets
out; this reads them back.

Nearest rather than only a hit, so a drag that runs off the end of the row
pins to the last mark instead of stopping at whatever it last touched, and
a pointer in the half-gap outside the first mark still answers.

members.name: handleDragStart
members.description:
Dragging across the marks draws a score, and letting go chooses it.

One press and a slide is how a rating is given on a phone, and on a desktop
it is how somebody who overshoots corrects without lifting. Pointer capture
is what makes it one gesture: without it the events go to whichever target
the pointer crossed into, and a drag that leaves the row stops reporting.

Nothing is chosen until release, so a drag that ends back where it started,
or off the element entirely, has asked for nothing.

members.description: Reports the value.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:
Which mark the row is drawn with.

`marks` is the star, and is what a rating means to most readers. `dots`
drops the glyph for a plain circle, which says how much rather than how
good: a star carries a judgement that a level of spice, a difficulty or a
confidence has not earned.

Both are one shape repeated and clipped to the score, so halves work in
either, and both are only a choice of drawing. A scale whose marks are
*different* drawings is a set of choices rather than a quantity: that is
`Radio.Group`, whose options already carry a value and a name each.

`appearance="marks"` onto every rating the server rendered, which React
held no prop for and reported as a hydration mismatch. The stylesheet was
already written the right way round, naming only `dots`, so marks is what
an unset one draws and nothing else had to move.

attributes.name: default-value
attributes.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

attributes.name: hint
attributes.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

attributes.name: feedback
attributes.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

attributes.name: required
attributes.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

attributes.name: max
attributes.description: How many marks there are.

attributes.name: step
attributes.description:
The smallest part of a mark that can be chosen.

`0.5` is the half star, and it is the reason the value is a number rather
than an index: with halves, five marks are ten answers.

attributes.name: readonly
attributes.description:
Whether this shows a score rather than asks for one.

A readout is not a control that has been switched off. It takes no focus,
answers no keys, and reads as one thing: see the note on the class.

attributes.name: value-text
attributes.description:
How the score is read out, where "3.5 out of 5" is not what it should say.

A rating out of five is one of the few places a screen reader gets a worse
answer from the value than from a sentence: "3.5" alone is a number without
a subject. This names the readout, where a control is named by its `label`
and each of its options by the score that option is.

attributes.name: show-value
attributes.description:
Whether the score is written out beside the marks.

Marks say roughly, and a number says exactly. Four and a bit stars is not a
reading anyone can repeat, which is why a product's average is nearly always
printed next to them. `Meter` spells its reading the same way and under the
same attribute.

It follows the pointer, because it labels what the marks are showing rather
than what the form holds: a label that disagreed with the marks under the
reader's own cursor would be worse than no label.

declarations.description:
A sandboxed `<iframe>` pointed at `src`, which is a document the consumer
provides. That document imports whatever the examples need, listens for a
render message, and writes the markup into itself.

**A frame rather than the page.** Rendering into the page meant an example
was styled by whatever surrounded it, which flatters the preview and lies
about it: an example that restyles `helix-card` restyled the sandbox too, a
script in an example ran against the real document, and a stray
`position: fixed` escaped the pane. It also left nothing to capture console
output from, and the terminal has to come from somewhere.

The cost is that the frame starts empty. Styles and element definitions do
not cross into it, because a document has its own stylesheets and a window
has its own custom element registry, so `src` has to load them. That is the
consumer's document rather than something guessed at here.

**The source is not trusted, and the frame is what makes that safe.**
`fullscreen` is granted for the same reason and found the same way: a video
in the preview offered a fullscreen button that did nothing at all, because
the policy default is `self`, this frame is not `self`, and a denied request
rejects a promise nobody was watching. Two capabilities now, both explicit,
both starred.

`allow="clipboard-write *"` is granted explicitly, and the star matters: the
policy defaults to `self` and this frame has an opaque origin, so it is not
`self` and the default denies it. A component inside the preview that copies
to the clipboard is otherwise a control that silently does nothing, which is
how this was found. Nothing else is granted, and a copy still needs the
reader's own gesture.

`sandbox="allow-scripts"` and no `allow-same-origin`, so the document runs on
an opaque origin: script in an example cannot reach this page, its storage,
its cookies, or the editor the source was typed into. Without it they could,
measured, through an `onerror` handler on an image that fails to load, which
`innerHTML` does not strip the way it refuses a `<script>` tag.

That is what lets a sandbox hold markup a reader pasted from somewhere, or
one day arrived in a shared link, rather than only what its owner typed.

`allow-forms` is granted because examples have forms in them and a submit
that silently does nothing is a worse lie than one that navigates a frame
nobody is looking at. Top-level navigation, popups and modals are not.

members.description: How the example is placed in the frame.

members.name: ready
members.description: Whether the frame has said it is listening.

members.name: handleMessage
members.description:
Takes messages from the frame.

Two checks, and both earn their place.

The window is the identity: `event.source` is a reference the sender cannot
forge, and this frame's `contentWindow` is one only this element holds.

The origin has to be opaque. The frame is sandboxed, so every message it
sends arrives as `"null"`, measured. A real origin therefore means the
frame is no longer showing the document it was given: `allow-scripts` lets
an example navigate its own frame, and whatever it navigated to inherits
`contentWindow` and could otherwise write lines into the terminal as though
the example had logged them.

members.name: target
members.description:
Where messages to the frame are addressed.

`'*'`, because there is nothing else to say: a sandboxed document has an
opaque origin and `postMessage` has no target string that names one.

It costs nothing. What is sent is the example's own source and stylesheet,
to the document that is about to render them, and that document is the one
thing on the page already entitled to both.

members.name: pending
members.description: Set while a coalesced send is waiting, so only one is ever queued.

members.name: scheduleSend
members.description:
Sends once the typing stops, replacing anything already waiting.

A frame was tried first and is the wrong unit. Keystrokes arrive fifty to a
hundred and fifty milliseconds apart, so each one lands in a frame of its
own and coalescing by frame coalesces nothing: the example was still being
rebuilt per character. The delay has to be longer than the gap between
keystrokes to catch a burst, and short enough to read as immediate when the
typing stops.

members.name: send
members.description: Sends the current source to the frame, once it is listening.

members.name: reload
members.description:
Loads the frame's document again, and re-sends the example to it.

For a bundle that has changed underneath a page nobody reloaded. The frame
carries its own build of the component library, as a classic script it ran
once at load, so a rebuilt bundle reaches a tab that is already open
exactly never: the sandbox around it hot-reloads and the preview inside it
keeps running whatever it started with, which reads as a component fix that
did not work.

Nothing needs to be resent by the caller. Clearing `ready` and reassigning
`src` puts this back in the state it was in before the first load, and the
new document announces itself the same way the first one did.

declarations.description:
Coordination is by event, the same way the accordion does it: a source pane
dispatches `SourceChange`, which bubbles, and the sandbox hands the value to
whatever preview is slotted into it. Neither child knows the other exists, so
either can be replaced or used alone.

The event carries the pane's `name`, which is what lets one sandbox hold
several panes without the root identifying senders by reference. `html` is
the preview's markup and `css` is its stylesheet. A pane named anything else
is showing something rather than driving it, and is ignored: the sandbox has
a pane rendering the example as JSX, and guessing would have put the text of
a React component into the preview.

**The dividers are two nested `helix-splitter`s, not a grid this element
drags itself.** It had its own: a five row grid, a stylesheet written to on
every pointer move, three pointer handlers, a keyboard handler reading which
axes each divider was allowed to move, and a corner placed by hand into the
cell where two tracks met. All of it is the splitter's now, including the
corner, which arrives on its own wherever a nested splitter crosses the one it
is in.

The panes are the inner splitter and the panel is the outer one, which is the
order that makes the panel span the full width: the outer divider runs edge to
edge and the inner stops at it.

**Both are controlled from here, so `split` and `panel-size` stay the truth.**
A splitter that owned its own position would leave this element reporting one
arrangement and showing another, and a consumer restoring a saved layout
writes to these two properties. Each splitter announces where it wants to go
and this answers, which is the same contract a form control has with a
framework.

**The panel is in pixels here and a percentage in the splitter, and the
conversion belongs here.** A terminal wants a number of lines rather than a
share of the window, so its height should not change when the window does. A
splitter has no business knowing that, so it stays percentage-pure and this
element, which does know what is in the panel, holds the box and converts.
That is also what keeps a stored `panelSize` from a previous visit meaning
what it meant when it was written.

members.name: lead
members.description:
Which pane comes first, before the divider.

A sandbox is read in one of two directions and the two are not a
preference. A workbench is a place to write, so the source leads and the
preview answers it. A reference page is a place to look, so the preview
leads and the source is what a reader opens if they want to know how it was
done. Same component, opposite reading order, and no consumer should have
to slot a preview into a hole named `source` to get it.

Not reflected, because no rule selects on it: the panes already carry
`data-pane`, which is what the stylesheet reaches for, and swapping the
names below keeps that true whichever way round they sit.

`split` follows the lead pane rather than the source, so `split="30"` means
the same thing in both directions: thirty percent to whatever comes first.

members.name: split
members.description: Percentage of the sandbox given to the source pane.

members.name: defaultSplit
members.description:
Where a reset puts the divider, where nothing declared it.

Separate from `split` for the reason `Splitter` keeps `default-position`
separate from `position`, and the bug is worth recording because this
element had it after that one was fixed. A double click reset to whatever
`split` held on the first render, which is the declared arrangement only
when nobody owns the property. The workbench owns it, restores it from the
address bar and from storage, so the first value it ever held was the
reader's last session: double clicking reset the sandbox to the size it
already was, which is to say it did nothing at all.

Declared rather than captured, so it is a number a consumer states and can
change, and it needs no first frame to be read on.

members.description:
What the panel's height becomes when it is closed.

Zero closes it outright. A panel whose contents include the control that
reopens it, a row of tabs being the usual one, wants that row left showing,
and only whoever slotted it knows how tall that is.

members.name: panelLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the panel's divider.

members.name: cornerLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the divider that moves both at once.

members.name: separatorLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the divider.

members.name: hasPanel
members.description:
Whether anything is in the panel region.

The divider above the panel is only meaningful when there is a panel to
size, and there is no way to ask in CSS: `:host(:has([slot="panel"]))` is
invalid, and the server has no children to look at. `slotchange` is the
platform answering on the client, which is where a divider is any use.

members.name: bodyHeight
members.description:
The body's height, which is what a pixel panel is a fraction of.

The panel is given in pixels and the splitter takes a percentage, so the two
only agree at one height: let the window change without recomputing and a
panel asked for at 192px quietly keeps whatever share of the old height that
was.

**Measured at render rather than cached from the observer**, which is the
second design here. The first held the number the observer last reported and
was correct only while the observer was firing, and a `ResizeObserver`
callback is delivered from the rendering lifecycle: a background tab runs
none, so the value went stale with nothing to say so. Reading the box at
render leaves one source of truth, and the observer's only job is to say
that a render is due.

Cheap, because renders are rare. A drag no longer goes through this element
at all: the splitter follows the pointer itself and announces once, when it
settles.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Asks for a render when the body changes size.

The box watched is the splitter itself, not the panel. Its size changes when
the window does and not when the divider moves, so answering it cannot feed
back into the position that answered it.

members.name: panelShare
members.description: The panel as a share of the body, which is what the splitter takes.

members.name: panelPosition
members.description:
Where the outer divider goes: everything the panel is not.

A hundred with no panel, which puts the divider on the floor of the sandbox
with the panes filling it. The line itself is hidden by the stylesheet in
that case, because a boundary needs two sides.

members.name: homePanelPosition
members.description: Where the panel divider goes on a reset, in the splitter's own units.

members.name: panelSliver
members.description: `panel-collapsed-size` in the units the splitter works in.

members.name: fromSource
members.description:
Whether a change came from inside this sandbox's source region.

Structural rather than a type check. It was `instanceof
HelixSandboxSource`, which was right until there was a second kind of
pane: the editor is `@helix-io/sandbox/editor`, on its own path because it
carries CodeMirror, and naming its class here would pull that back into
this module for every consumer. Where the event came from is a question
about the tree, and the tree can answer it.

members.name: handleSourceChange
members.description:
Takes a change from one of this sandbox's own source panes.

The origin is checked, and has to be. `helix-change` bubbles and composes,
so anything a consumer slots into a sandbox sends one up here too. A
sandbox hears a great deal that is not its source.

members.name: handleCaret
members.description:
Writes the cursor position onto any status bar slotted here.

The same shape as the source-to-preview hand-off, and for the same reason:
the editor and the bar never speak, so either can be absent. It goes
straight to the element rather than through a property a framework owns,
because this fires on every keystroke and every arrow press.

members.name: parts
members.description:
The parts of this sandbox it drives, wherever they sit inside it.

Descendants, not children. A preview and a status bar happen to be slotted
directly, but a terminal lives inside the tab set that holds the panel, so
a search of `children` found none and the console went nowhere. Where a
consumer nests a pane is their arrangement to make.

Client only: the server has no children to read.

members.name: handleConsole
members.description:
Hands a console line from the preview to any terminal slotted here.

Every `helix-console` is forwarded, with no check on where it came from.
Unlike a change, which any form control in a sandbox emits, this event is
dispatched by exactly one thing: a preview relaying what the document
inside its frame wrote. There is nothing else here it could be confused
with.

members.name: axis
members.description:
The orientation in force.

Unset is horizontal, and stays unset: the default is the absent attribute,
so a reflected default cannot appear on the host after hydration.

members.name: settled
members.description:
Says the arrangement has settled, so a consumer can keep it.

When it settles, not while it moves. A drag is a stream of positions and
only the one it ends at is a preference; announcing each would ask whoever
is listening to write to storage a hundred times to record one decision.

The sandbox does not keep it. Where a preference lives, and whether it
should be kept at all, is the consumer's to decide, and a component that
wrote to storage on its own would be deciding for all of them under a key
it chose.

members.name: handlePanesChange
members.description:
Answers a divider that has asked to move.

Both splitters are controlled from here, so neither applies anything on its
own: each announces where it wants to go and this decides. That is what
keeps `split` and `panelSize` the truth about the arrangement rather than a
stale copy of it.

`target` against `currentTarget`, because a source pane's own change bubbles
up through these same elements on its way to the host. Only a splitter
speaking for itself is one of ours, and only those are stopped: the sandbox
announces `arrangement` and a consumer never sees the two inside it.

members.name: watchBody
members.description: Watches the body, whose height is what the pane sizes are computed from.

members.name: readPanel
members.description:
Notes whether there is a panel, which is what its dividers depend on.

Asked of the light DOM rather than of the slot. `slotchange` is the event
that says it changed, and it is listened for, but it is not the only way
to know: a sandbox whose panel was in the markup all along has nothing to
change, and an environment that does not dispatch the event at all leaves
the dividers permanently absent. What is slotted into a named slot is a
question the host can answer directly.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-base-pagination-size` composes `helix-base-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/web` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.
